subject: Computing
source: Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2 specification (Topic 1 Computational thinking, Topic 6 Problem solving with programming; Python and pseudo-code, no non-exam assessment), sequence informed by the school's Drive Y10-11 scheme (1 Fundamentals of Algorithms, 2A Programming Basics) and Y9 Programming basics lesson plan | Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2 specification (syllabus file content/syllabus/ks4/computing.json: units 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 6.1 to 6.6; Python 3). Original lessons. The existing y10 set (content/lessons/computing/y10.json) already introduces decomposition and abstraction, flowcharts, pseudo-code and trace tables, linear and binary search, bubble and merge sort, and Python variables, validation, lists and strings; these lessons do not re-teach those and instead cover the remaining spec points, add code tracing, efficiency and exam-style practice.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Decomposition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking
objectives: Define and apply decomposition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking
Decompose a problem into smaller sub-problems
Identify which details to keep and which to ignore (abstraction)

keywords.def: a way of solving problems using decomposition, abstraction and algorithms
breaking a problem into smaller, manageable parts
removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters
a sequence of steps or rules to solve a problem

starter: Bismillah. Define the term algorithm in one sentence.
Write the steps to make a cup of tea, as an algorithm, in under 6 steps.
Why does a map of the London Underground leave out most of the real geography?

teach.heading: Computational thinking
bullets: Decomposition: break the problem down.
Abstraction: focus on the important detail.
Algorithmic thinking: write clear steps.
teach.note: Introduce the three skills as the toolkit for the whole course; Paper 2 asks you to apply computational thinking to problems. Pose the question: how would you design a prayer-times app? Collect ideas, then organise them.

teach.heading: Decomposition example
bullets: Problem: a quiz app.
Sub-problem 1: store questions.
Sub-problem 2: ask and check answers.
Sub-problem 3: keep score and show result.
teach.note: Show the tree diagram. Benefits: easier to understand, different people can work on each part, parts can be tested separately and reused. A common mistake in exams is to give a generic answer; always relate to the scenario in the question.

teach.heading: Abstraction example
bullets: Tube map: stations and lines only.
Ignore distances and street layout.
Simpler model, easier to use.
teach.note: Ask pupils what a satnav needs and ignores (it needs roads, speed limits; it ignores the colour of buildings). Define abstraction exactly: filtering out details we do not need so we can focus on the problem. Another example is a variable representing a value.

teach.heading: Algorithmic thinking
bullets: Work out the steps in order.
Decide the inputs, processes and outputs.
Plan before coding.
teach.note: Model an input-process-output table for 'calculate the average of three marks': inputs mark1, mark2, mark3; process add and divide by 3; output the average. Exams often ask you to identify inputs, processes and outputs.

practice: Decompose the problem 'create a program to run a school canteen till' into at least three sub-problems.
A bus route map shows stops and numbers but not the exact bends in the road. Which computational thinking skill is this?
State one benefit of decomposition for a team creating a game.
independent: Decompose the problem of a program that manages a mosque's weekly timetable. Draw a tree diagram with at least three levels.
List the details to keep and details to ignore when abstracting a model of a car park for a ticket machine.
Write an input-process-output table for a program that calculates the cost of a taxi journey from miles and price per mile.
exit: Define abstraction.
Give one reason for using decomposition when writing a large program.
lessons.homework: Choose a real system (such as an online shop). Describe how it could be decomposed and what abstractions it uses. Write 150 words.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a tree diagram template and sentence stems ('This is abstraction because...'). Stretch: evaluate whether a given abstraction has removed too much detail.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Flowcharts
objectives: Use the standard flowchart symbols correctly
Interpret and complete a flowchart for an algorithm
Create a flowchart for a problem with selection and iteration

keywords.def: a diagram showing the steps of an algorithm using standard symbols
oval symbol marking start or end
diamond symbol with two exits, yes and no
rectangle symbol for an action or calculation
parallelogram symbol for data entering or leaving

starter: Bismillah. State the three parts of computational thinking.
Which flowchart symbol is used for a yes/no question?
What is the difference between selection and iteration?

teach.heading: Flowchart symbols
bullets: Oval: start/end.
Parallelogram: input/output.
Rectangle: process.
Diamond: decision.
Arrows show the flow.
teach.note: Use the Edexcel-style symbols. Remind pupils that arrows show direction and that each diamond must have two labelled exits (Yes/No). Marks are lost for unlabelled decisions.

teach.heading: Selection in a flowchart
bullets: Start.
Input n.
Decision: n MOD 2 = 0?
Yes: output 'even'. No: output 'odd'. End.
teach.note: Draw this step by step. Trace with n = 7 (odd) and n = 10 (even). Ask what MOD does. Link to Y9 learning: remainders. Use the phrase 'follow the arrows' when tracing.

teach.heading: Iteration in a flowchart
bullets: Set total to 0 and count to 1.
Decision: count <= 5?
Yes: add count to total, add 1 to count, loop back.
No: output total.
teach.note: Show how a loop is made by an arrow going back to a decision. Trace this algorithm: it outputs 15. Ask pupils what it calculates (sum of 1 to 5). A common mistake is forgetting to increase the counter, causing an infinite loop.

teach.heading: Exam technique
bullets: Use a ruler and correct shapes.
Start with a terminator.
Label Yes/No.
Check by tracing.
teach.note: Teach pupils to check any flowchart they draw using test data. Mention that on Paper 1 they may need to complete missing parts of a flowchart or say what the algorithm does. Use command words: 'complete', 'describe', 'state'.

practice: Which symbol would you use for 'Input the user's age'? (parallelogram)
Trace the sum flowchart. What are the values of count and total at each pass? (count 1,2,3,4,5; total 1,3,6,10,15)
Add the missing labels to a decision diamond which asks 'Is the temperature above 30?'
independent: Draw a flowchart for an algorithm that inputs a mark and outputs 'Pass' if it is 40 or more, otherwise 'Fail'.
Draw a flowchart which asks for numbers repeatedly until the user enters 0, then outputs how many numbers were entered (not counting 0).
Trace your flowchart with test data 5, 8, 2, 0 and write down the final output.
exit: Name the shape used for a decision and explain what must be on its exits.
State the output of the sum flowchart if the limit changes from 5 to 4.
lessons.homework: Draw a flowchart for an algorithm that asks for a password up to 3 times and ends with 'Locked' if all attempts are wrong.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide symbol stencils and partly completed flowcharts. Stretch: draw a flowchart with a nested decision for a ticket price calculator.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Pseudo-code and trace tables
objectives: Read and write algorithms in pseudo-code using sequence, selection and iteration
Complete a trace table for an algorithm
Identify the purpose of an algorithm and find errors

keywords.def: a way of writing algorithms in structured English not tied to a programming language
a table used to record the values of variables as an algorithm runs
a named store whose value can change
a mistake that makes a program run but give the wrong result

starter: Bismillah. Draw the symbol for a decision.
Why is a flowchart useful before coding?
What is the value of 17 MOD 5?

teach.heading: What is pseudo-code?
bullets: Structured English for algorithms.
No strict syntax, but be clear.
Uses SET/IF/WHILE-type keywords.
teach.note: Explain that Pearson's papers present algorithms in pseudo-code (and flowcharts) and that you should check the specification's conventions for the exact style; clear, consistent structure is what matters. Show how to write assignments, inputs and outputs. Keep to one style throughout.

teach.heading: Pseudo-code example
bullets: SET total TO 0
FOR i FROM 1 TO 4
SET total TO total + i * 2
OUTPUT total
teach.note: Walk through the algorithm: i = 1 → total 2; i = 2 → total 6; i = 3 → total 12; i = 4 → total 20. Present the trace table with the columns i and total. Pupils should fill the table as you go and see that the output is 20.

teach.heading: Trace tables
bullets: One column for each variable.
One row for each change.
Output column for printed values.
teach.note: Show a second example with selection: SET x TO 12, IF x MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT 'even' ELSE OUTPUT 'odd'. Teach pupils to record every change and not to skip rows. Common mistake: updating two variables on one row when they change at different steps.

teach.heading: Purpose and errors
bullets: Trace with simple test data.
State what it does in one sentence.
Look for off-by-one and wrong operators.
teach.note: Give an algorithm that finds the largest of three numbers with a bug (uses < instead of >). Trace it with 5, 9, 2 to show the wrong result. Explain syntax errors vs logic errors. Discuss how testing with boundary data finds errors.

practice: Trace: SET a TO 3; SET b TO 4; SET c TO a * b; SET a TO c - a; OUTPUT a. (a = 9)
State the purpose: SET count TO 0; FOR i FROM 1 TO 10; IF i MOD 2 = 0 THEN SET count TO count + 1; OUTPUT count. (counts even numbers from 1 to 10, outputs 5)
Spot the error: an algorithm meant to output the highest of two numbers outputs the lower one.
independent: Complete a trace table for: SET n TO 5; SET f TO 1; WHILE n > 1; SET f TO f * n; SET n TO n - 1; END WHILE; OUTPUT f. (output 120)
Write pseudo-code that inputs 3 numbers and outputs the largest.
Write pseudo-code to output the total of the numbers 1 to 100, and state the expected answer (5050).
exit: What is the purpose of a trace table?
State the output of: SET x TO 2; FOR i FROM 1 TO 3; SET x TO x * 2; OUTPUT x. (16)
lessons.homework: Write pseudo-code for a program which asks for 5 test marks and outputs the average. Trace it with 60, 70, 80, 90, 100.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide trace table templates and pre-filled first rows; use colour to track variables. Stretch: find and correct two errors in an unfamiliar pseudo-code algorithm.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Searching algorithms: linear and binary search
objectives: Describe and carry out a linear search
Describe and carry out a binary search on a sorted list
Compare the two searches and choose the right one

keywords.def: checks each item in turn from the start until the target is found or the list ends
repeatedly checks the middle item of a sorted list and halves the search area
arranged in order, such as lowest to highest
how few steps or how little time or memory an algorithm needs

starter: Bismillah. Trace: SET x TO 3; SET x TO x + 4; OUTPUT x.
How do you look up a name in a printed phone book?
What does 'sorted' mean for a list of numbers?

teach.heading: Linear search
bullets: Start at the first item.
Compare each item with the target.
Stop when found or at the end.
teach.note: Search [14, 9, 22, 5, 17] for 22: compare 14, 9, 22 found at the third position (3 comparisons). Search for 30: all 5 compared, not found. Note it works on any list, sorted or not.

teach.heading: Binary search idea
bullets: The list must be sorted.
Check the middle item.
Target smaller? Discard the right half.
Target bigger? Discard the left half.
teach.note: Link to guessing a number between 1 and 100 and being told higher or lower. State the rule for a list with an even number of items: pick a consistent middle (e.g. the lower middle) and follow it, which is acceptable as long as it is clear. Misconception: binary search works on unsorted lists; it does not.

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Target 27. Middle: 21 (position 5).
Middle (lower): 34. 27 < 34, so search 27. Found.
teach.note: Draw the list as boxes and cross out the discarded half each time. Count comparisons: 3 for binary against 6 for linear. Show how with 1,000,000 items binary search needs about 20 comparisons at most. State that this is why sorted data is valuable.

teach.heading: Choosing a search
bullets: Unsorted list: linear.
Sorted and large: binary.
Binary needs fewer comparisons.
Sorting first costs time.
teach.note: Pose a scenario: a list of 10 names unsorted versus 1 million sorted student IDs. Ask which search to choose and why. Exam answers should compare efficiency and the requirement for sorted data.

practice: Linear search for 5 in [8, 3, 5, 9]. How many comparisons? (3)
Why can't you use binary search on [9, 2, 7, 4]? (not sorted)
Binary search for 12 in [2, 5, 9, 12, 15, 20, 31]. Which item is checked first? (12, the middle item, found immediately)
independent: Carry out a linear search for 40 in [52, 12, 40, 8, 27] and record each comparison.
Carry out a binary search for 8 in [3, 8, 12, 15, 21, 27, 34, 40, 52] showing low, high and middle each time.
Write a paragraph comparing linear and binary search, with one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
exit: State one requirement for using binary search.
Which search is usually faster on a large sorted list, and why?
lessons.homework: Write pseudo-code for a linear search that outputs the position of a target in a list or 'not found'. Test with two lists.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide cards to physically cross out halves; show each step in colour. Stretch: work out the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs for 31 items (5).

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Sorting algorithms: bubble sort
objectives: Describe how a bubble sort works
Carry out a bubble sort on a list, showing each pass
Explain when the algorithm can stop

keywords.def: arrange data in order
compares neighbouring items and swaps them if out of order, repeating passes
one complete run through the list
exchange the positions of two items

starter: Bismillah. Name the two searches we studied and state when binary search can be used.
Put these in order: 7, 2, 9, 4.
Explain how you physically sorted a hand of cards when you last played a card game.

teach.heading: Why sort?
bullets: Sorted data is easier to search.
Used in contacts, scores and files.
Different algorithms sort differently.
teach.note: Ask for examples of sorted data in apps (alphabetical contacts, leaderboards). Explain we need precise instructions for a computer to sort.

teach.heading: How bubble sort works
bullets: Compare the first two items.
Swap if they are in the wrong order.
Move along one place and repeat.
Repeat passes until no swaps.
teach.note: Demonstrate with 5 pupils holding number cards or with number cards on screen. Largest values 'bubble' to the end. After pass 1 the largest item is in its final position.

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Start: 5 3 8 1.
Pass 3: 1 3 5 8. Pass 4: no swaps, stop.
teach.note: Show every comparison in pass 1: compare 5, 3 swap giving 3 5 8 1; compare 5, 8 no swap; compare 8, 1 swap giving 3 5 1 8. Count swaps per pass. A common mistake is to stop after pass 3 without a final pass proving no swaps are needed (but accept if all in place and explain).

teach.heading: Strengths and weaknesses
bullets: Simple to understand and code.
Needs many passes on big lists.
Slow compared with merge sort.
teach.note: Compare: for n items bubble sort may need around n × n comparisons. Do not require formulas at GCSE, but pupils should state it is inefficient for large lists. Use a flag: if no swaps in a pass, stop early.

practice: Carry out pass 1 of a bubble sort on 4, 2, 7, 1. (2 4 1 7)
How many swaps happen in pass 1 on 3, 2, 1? (2) What is the list after pass 1? (2 1 3)
How does the algorithm know it is finished?
independent: Bubble sort 9, 4, 7, 2, 6, writing the list after each pass and the number of swaps.
Write pseudo-code for one pass of a bubble sort on a list called nums with n items.
Explain two weaknesses of bubble sort for a list of one million items.
exit: State what happens in a bubble sort when two neighbouring items are in the wrong order.
After one pass of 6, 5, 1, 4 what is the list? (5 1 4 6)
lessons.homework: Bubble sort the list 12, 5, 9, 1, 8 and show every pass. Explain how you know when to stop.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use physical number cards and highlighters to mark the pair being compared. Stretch: describe how a flag variable could stop the sort early.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Computational thinking (Topic 1)
lessons.title: Sorting algorithms: merge sort and comparing sorts
objectives: Describe how a merge sort splits and merges lists
Carry out a merge sort on a list of 8 items
Compare bubble sort and merge sort

keywords.def: splits a list into single items, then merges them back in order
solving a problem by splitting it into smaller problems
combine two sorted lists into one sorted list
storage used while the algorithm is running

starter: Bismillah. After one pass of bubble sort on 4, 3, 2, 1 what is the list? (3 2 1 4)
Why does bubble sort slow down on large lists?
How would you sort a pile of 100 exam papers with the help of 3 friends?

teach.heading: Split then merge
bullets: Keep splitting the list in half.
Stop at lists of one item.
Merge pairs of lists back in order.
teach.note: Introduce merge sort as a divide and conquer algorithm and link to decomposition. A list of one item is already sorted. Show the stages with arrows.

teach.heading: Splitting
teach.note: Draw the split tree. Emphasise that no sorting happens while splitting; it all happens during merging. Common mistake: trying to sort during the split stage.

teach.heading: Merging
bullets: Compare the first items of each list.
Move the smaller one to the new list.
Repeat until both lists are used.
teach.note: Merge 6 and 2 to get 2 6; 8 and 4 to get 4 8; 3 and 7 to get 3 7; 1 and 5 to get 1 5. Then merge 2 6 with 4 8: compare 2 and 4, take 2; compare 6 and 4, take 4; compare 6 and 8, take 6; then 8: result 2 4 6 8. Merge 3 7 with 1 5: 1 3 5 7. Final merge gives 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8.

teach.heading: Bubble vs merge
bullets: Merge sort is faster on large lists.
Merge sort needs extra memory.
Bubble sort is simpler to write.
teach.note: Give exam-style comparison language: merge sort is more efficient (fewer comparisons) for large data sets but uses more memory because it creates new lists; bubble sort is simple but slow. Ask pupils to decide for a list of 10 items versus 10 million.

practice: Merge the sorted lists 2 5 9 and 1 6 8. (1 2 5 6 8 9)
Split 7 3 9 1 5 2 into halves and halves again. (7 3 9 | 1 5 2 then 7 | 3 9 | 1 | 5 2 and so on)
State one advantage and one disadvantage of merge sort.
independent: Merge sort 9, 3, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 4, showing the split and merge stages in a diagram.
Compare bubble sort and merge sort in a table with three rows: how it works, speed on large lists, memory use.
Write a 4-mark answer: 'Explain which sorting algorithm would be better for sorting 1 million customer records.'
exit: What does a merge sort do first?
Give one reason merge sort needs more memory than bubble sort.
lessons.homework: Merge sort the list 14, 3, 9, 20, 1, 7 and show your working. Then explain why merge sort is a divide and conquer algorithm.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a split-and-merge template with boxes; use number cards. Stretch: count the comparisons used in your merge sort and compare with a bubble sort of the same list.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Programming in Python (Topic 6)
lessons.title: Python: variables, data types, operators and validation
objectives: Use variables, constants and the five main data types in Python
Use arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, including // and %
Write a program that validates input with a loop

keywords.def: a named value that does not change while a program runs
converting a value from one data type to another
checking that data is sensible and in the allowed range before using it
a mistake that breaks the rules of the language so the program cannot run

starter: Bismillah. State the data type of: 5, '5', 5.0, True.
What is 29 // 6 and 29 % 6? (4 and 5)
Which loop do you use when you do not know how many repeats are needed?

teach.heading: Variables and constants
bullets: Variables change; constants do not.
Use meaningful names: price_per_item.
Python style for a constant: VAT_RATE = 0.2.
teach.note: Python has no true constants, but writing in capital letters shows the value should not be changed. Explain why named constants help: changing one line updates the whole program. Show how a bad name like x makes code hard to read.

teach.heading: Casting and operators
bullets: int(), float(), str() change types.
Arithmetic: + - * / // % **.
Comparison: == != < > <= >=.
Logical: and, or, not.
teach.note: Run the code to find a worker's wages: hours = float(input('Hours? ')), rate = 12.50, pay = hours * rate. Predict the output for 8 hours (100.0). Remind pupils that input returns a string.

teach.heading: Validation with while
bullets: Ask for input.
While it is invalid: show message, ask again.
Continue when valid.
teach.note: Code: age = int(input('Age (0-120)? ')); while age < 0 or age > 120: print('Invalid'); age = int(input('Age (0-120)? ')). Distinguish validation (sensible data) from verification (correct data, such as typing a password twice). Discuss what happens if the user types letters: ValueError; show try/except only as an extension.

teach.heading: Testing
bullets: Normal data: 25.
Boundary data: 0, 120, -1, 121.
Erroneous data: 'abc'.
teach.note: Teach test data types and have pupils write a test table with expected result. Exams (Paper 2) reward programs that handle boundaries correctly. Model running tests and recording results.

practice: Write the Python to store a constant PI as 3.14.
What is the output? x = 17; print(x // 5); print(x % 5); print(x / 5). (3, 2, 3.4)
Write a condition that is True when age is between 11 and 16 inclusive. (age >= 11 and age <= 16)
independent: Write a program which asks for a price and a quantity, uses a constant for VAT at 20 per cent, and outputs the total including VAT.
Write a program that asks for a mark from 0 to 100 and keeps asking until a valid mark is entered.
Create a test table with normal, boundary and erroneous data for your mark program.
exit: What is the difference between validation and verification?
Name one example each of normal, boundary and erroneous test data for an age between 0 and 120.
lessons.homework: Write and test a Python program that converts a number of minutes into hours and minutes and validates the input is not negative.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide code with comments and blanks and a data type glossary. Stretch: use try and except to handle non-numeric input without crashing.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Programming in Python (Topic 6)
lessons.title: Python: lists, strings and implementing a search
objectives: Create, index and loop through a list in Python
Use common string operations such as len and slicing
Implement a linear search in Python

keywords.def: an ordered collection of items stored under one name
the position of an item in a list, starting at 0
the number of items in a list or characters in a string, found with len()
part of a string

starter: Bismillah. Write a for loop which prints the numbers 1 to 5.
Which search needs a sorted list?
What data type is 'Quran'?

teach.heading: Lists
bullets: names = ['Amina', 'Bilal', 'Sara'].
names[0] is 'Amina'.
len(names) is 3.
names.append('Omar') adds an item.
teach.note: Stress that indexes start at 0, a very common source of off-by-one errors. Ask what names[3] would be after the append (Omar) and what it was before (error: index out of range).

teach.heading: Looping through lists
bullets: for name in names: print(name).
for i in range(len(names)): uses the index.
Total: total = total + marks[i].
teach.note: Show both loop styles. Use the index loop when position matters, e.g. printing position numbers. Calculate the total and mean of the list [60, 72, 85, 91] (308 and 77.0).

teach.heading: Strings
bullets: len('Quran') is 5.
word[0] is the first letter.
word[1:4] slices characters 1 to 3.
word.upper() makes capitals.
teach.note: Demonstrate slicing: 'Madinah'[0:3] = 'Mad'. Strings can be indexed but not changed in place. Link to ASCII later in the Data topic.

teach.heading: Linear search in Python
bullets: found = False
for i in range(len(nums)):
if nums[i] == target: found = True
print position or 'not found'.
teach.note: Write the program together and test with [14, 9, 22, 5, 17] and the target 22 (position 2 as index; position 3 counting from 1). Test with a target that is not present. Compare with the pseudo-code from lesson 4 and note the matching structure.

practice: Given marks = [45, 60, 72, 88], what is marks[2] and len(marks)? (72, 4)
What does 'Computer'[0:3] give? ('Com')
Complete the loop to add all items of marks into total.
independent: Write a program that stores 5 names in a list, then asks the user for a name and says whether it is in the list using a linear search.
Write a program that finds the largest number in a list of 6 numbers without using max().
Stretch: write a program that counts how many vowels are in a word typed by the user.
exit: What is the index of the first item in a Python list?
Write the Python expression for the number of items in a list called scores.
lessons.homework: Write a Python program which asks the user for 5 marks, stores them in a list, then prints the total, average and highest mark.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide code with comments to match to descriptions, and colour index positions on a list diagram. Stretch: implement a bubble sort in Python for a list of 6 numbers.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.1: Computational thinking: decomposition, abstraction and subprograms
lessons.title: Decomposition, abstraction and subprograms: modelling a problem
lessons.bigQuestion: How do programmers solve a problem that is too big to hold in one head?
objectives: Explain how decomposition and abstraction are used to model a problem (1.1.1)
Decompose a scenario into sub-problems with inputs and outputs
Explain the benefits of using subprograms (1.1.2)
successCriteria: All: define decomposition and abstraction and give one example of each
Most: decompose a scenario and say which details a model keeps and ignores
Some: justify the use of subprograms in a given program using three distinct benefits
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: maps and models leave out detail on purpose
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah (trust) in building software others will rely on: a well-structured program is easier to check and keep honest

keywords.def: breaking a problem into smaller parts that can be solved separately
removing detail that is not needed so you focus on what matters
a simplified representation of a real system, built using abstraction
a named block of code that does one job and can be called many times

starter: Bismillah. Name the three skills of computational thinking.
A Tube map ignores real distances. State one reason that is helpful to passengers.
In Python, what does def do?

teach.heading: Decomposition: divide the problem
bullets: Break a big problem into smaller sub-problems
Solve and test each part on its own
Then join the parts together
teach.note: Use a prayer-times app as the running scenario. Ask pupils to shout out tasks; group them on the board. Stress that each sub-problem should be small enough to describe in one sentence. Pupils often list features; push them to say what goes in and what comes out of each part.

head: Sub-problem
Input
Output
rows: Name and time of next prayer

teach.heading: Abstraction: keep what matters
bullets: Decide which details the solution needs
Ignore the rest
The result is a simpler model
teach.note: Define a model as a simplified version of the real thing. The key exam skill is to name specific details kept and ignored in the scenario, not to write general sentences. Note that abstraction is not hiding code from users; it is leaving detail out of the problem description.

teach.heading: Worked example: model a lift
teach.note: Model aloud (I do). Show that decomposition splits the job and abstraction chooses the data. Ask: what would we add if the lift must carry a stretcher? Link to 'fitness for purpose'.

model.problem: A programmer is asked to write the control program for a lift in a three-storey school. Decompose the problem and state what the model leaves out.
steps: Sub-problem 1: read which floor button was pressed (input: button number)
Sub-problem 2: decide direction (input: current floor and target floor; output: up or down)
Sub-problem 3: move the lift and stop at the floor (output: motor command)
Sub-problem 4: open and close the doors
Model keeps: current floor, target floor, door state. It ignores: the colour of the lift, who is inside, the music
model.answer: Four sub-problems, each with clear inputs and outputs, and a model that stores only the data the control program needs.

teach.heading: Subprograms: name it once, use it often
bullets: A subprogram is a named block with one job
Call it whenever you need that job done
Place the logic in one place only
teach.note: Trace the code with pupils: the function vat is defined once, then called twice. Ask what would change if the VAT rate changed: only one line. List benefits: avoids repeating code, shorter programs, easier to test and debug, easier to maintain, parts can be shared by a team, and can be reused in other programs.

teach.heading: Check: benefits of subprograms
teach.note: Whiteboards up on the count of three. Option C is the trap: subprograms do not make code run faster in themselves. Option A describes a benefit that is about repetition. Ask pupils why D is true but not the best answer here.

check.q: A program calculates VAT in five different places. Which is the best reason to move the calculation into one subprogram?
options: It stops the program having any errors
A change to the VAT rule is made in one place only
It makes the program run much faster
It means the program no longer needs variables
check.why: Reuse and easier maintenance: changing the rule once fixes every call. A subprogram does not remove errors (A), does not by itself speed the code up (C) and variables are still needed (D).

practice: A mosque wants a program to manage its weekly rota for volunteers. Write four sub-problems and, for each, one input and one output.
A satnav model of a road network keeps road names, lengths and speed limits. State two details it ignores and say why that is acceptable.
A game draws an enemy character in eight different places. Explain how a subprogram would help.
independent: Core: Decompose the problem 'a school canteen till' into at least four sub-problems. Next to each, name the data it needs.
Extend: Write two examples of abstraction in a model of a school timetable. For each, say what is kept and what is ignored.
Stretch: A team of three writes a library loans program. Use decomposition and subprograms to explain how the work could be shared and tested, in about 100 words.
exit: Define abstraction and give one example not used today.
Give two benefits of using subprograms in a large program.
lessons.homework: Choose a program you use (a bus app, a game or a banking app). Write 120 words on how it could be decomposed and what abstraction its model uses.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a blank three-column table (sub-problem, input, output) and sentence stems such as 'The model ignores ... because ...'. Stretch: evaluate a model that has ignored too much detail and say what to add. Builds on y10 lesson 1, which introduced the terms; this lesson applies them to modelling and adds subprograms (1.1.2).

lessons.unit: Unit 1.2: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
lessons.title: Algorithm building blocks: sequence, selection, repetition and iteration
lessons.bigQuestion: Which three ideas are enough to build almost any algorithm?
objectives: Identify sequence, selection and repetition in an algorithm (1.2.1)
Distinguish count-controlled and condition-controlled repetition
Write an algorithm that iterates over a data structure
successCriteria: All: name the construct used in a short algorithm
Most: write a loop that processes every item of a list
Some: combine selection inside a loop to count or total items meeting a rule
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: sequences, repeated calculation and conditions
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and care in checking work step by step

keywords.def: instructions carried out one after another in order
choosing which instructions to run, based on a condition
running instructions more than once, in a loop
going through each item of a data structure, one at a time

starter: Bismillah. What does a diamond mean in a flowchart?
Write one line of Python that stores your name in a variable.
Say in words what for i in range(3): print(i) prints.

teach.heading: Three constructs
bullets: Sequence: step after step, in order
Selection: if / elif / else chooses a path
Repetition: a loop runs steps again
teach.note: Every algorithm in the course, from bubble sort to a login check, is made from these. Show each as a flowchart shape: a straight line, a diamond with two exits, a diamond with a line looping back. Point out that each block has one entry and one exit.

teach.heading: Two kinds of repetition
bullets: Count-controlled: repeat a set number of times
Condition-controlled: repeat until a test is met
Choose for when the count is known, while when it is not
teach.note: Run both programs. The for loop knows it will run 4 times; the while loop stops when the total reaches 10 or more, and that depends on the values. Ask pupils what happens if the condition never becomes false: an infinite loop.

code.text:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total = total + n
print(total)

stock = 20
weeks = 0
while stock > 0:
    stock = stock - 6
    weeks = weeks + 1
print(weeks)

teach.heading: Iteration over a data structure
bullets: Visit every item of a list in turn
Selection inside the loop filters items
Variables such as count store the result
teach.note: The loop variable takes each value of the list in turn; there is no index to manage. Point out that the if is inside the loop because it must be asked about every item. Pupils often put count = 0 inside the loop; show why that resets it each time.

teach.heading: Worked example: highest mark
teach.note: Model the thinking: set the first item as the highest so far, then compare each other item. Check with the trace: 45 -> 72 -> 72 -> 72 -> 90. Ask pupils why we do not start the highest at 0 (it fails for negative data, and starting with an item in the list is safer).

model.problem: Write pseudocode that outputs the highest value in the list temps = [14, 19, 11, 22, 17].
steps: Set highest to the first item, temps[0] (14)
FOR each t IN temps: compare t with highest
IF t > highest THEN set highest to t
After the loop ends, OUTPUT highest
model.answer: highest = 14, 19, 19, 22, 22, so the output is 22. It uses sequence, iteration over the list and selection inside it.

teach.heading: Check: which construct?
teach.note: Answer B. A is selection, C sequence, D a count-controlled loop. Ask pupils to say what the output is when the loop has run (the running total each time). A common slip is to call any loop 'selection' because it has a condition.

check.q: An algorithm asks for passwords until the user types the correct one. Which construct repeats the question?
check.why: The number of attempts is unknown in advance, so the loop is controlled by a condition. A count-controlled loop (D) needs a known number of repeats; selection (C) chooses but does not repeat.

practice: Name the construct in each: (a) IF age >= 18 THEN OUTPUT 'adult'; (b) FOR 1 TO 7 OUTPUT 'Salam'; (c) SET a TO 3 then SET b TO a + 2.
Write pseudocode that totals the prices in the list [2.50, 1.20, 0.80] using iteration.
Rewrite the while loop in the lesson (stock = 20, minus 6 each week) as a flowchart description with a decision diamond.
independent: Core: Write pseudocode to count how many names in a list of ten begin with the letter A.
Extend: Write a Python program that loops over a list of marks, outputs the mean and the number of marks above the mean.
Stretch: Describe an algorithm that checks whether every number in a list is bigger than the one before it. State which constructs you used.
exit: State the difference between count-controlled and condition-controlled repetition.
Which construct is used when a program chooses between two outputs? Give an example.
lessons.homework: Write an algorithm in pseudocode for a till that adds the prices in a list until the total passes 20 pounds. State which constructs you used.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give colour-coded cards (sequence blue, selection green, repetition orange) to sort lines of an algorithm. Stretch: write the loop in two ways, with for and with while.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.2: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
lessons.title: Variables, constants, strings, records and arrays
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we store many pieces of related data so a program can find them again?
objectives: Use variables, constants and strings in algorithms (1.2.2)
Describe and use records
Read and write values in one- and two-dimensional arrays
successCriteria: All: explain the difference between a variable and a constant
Most: use an index to read an item from a 1D array and from a 2D array
Some: choose between a record and an array for a given set of data and justify it
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: coordinates and tables of data
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah in keeping data about people accurate and organised

keywords.def: a named value that cannot change while the program runs
a group of related fields, possibly of different types, about one thing
a fixed-size collection of items of the same type, accessed by index
the position number of an item in an array, starting at 0
an array of arrays, accessed with a row and a column index

starter: Bismillah. What is the output of 7 // 2 in Python?
What is the data type of '25' with the quotation marks?
Name the two parts of a linear search loop: what is compared, and when does it stop?

teach.heading: Variables, constants and strings
bullets: Variable: named storage whose value can change
Constant: a fixed value, such as VAT_RATE
String: a sequence of characters, such as a name
teach.note: Ask why a constant is better than typing 0.2 each time: one change updates everywhere, and the name explains the number. Python has no true constants; by convention we write the name in capitals. Strings: remind pupils that quotation marks make a string, and that numbers inside quotes cannot be added.

code.text:
VAT_RATE = 0.2
price = 30
name = "Amina"
price = price + price * VAT_RATE
print(name, "pays", price)

teach.heading: Records
bullets: A record groups related fields about one item
Fields can have different data types
Use a name for each field
teach.note: Contrast with arrays: one student has a string name, an integer age and a Boolean. In Python we can store a record as a dictionary. Show how record['name'] reads one field. Ask what a list of records would look like (one record per student).

teach.heading: Arrays and 2D arrays
bullets: 1D array: one row of items, index from 0
2D array: rows and columns, two indexes
Write grid[row][column]
teach.note: Draw the grid on the board and number rows and columns from 0. Pupils reverse row and column constantly: say 'row first, then column' as a chant. Note an array is fixed-size and holds one type, and that Python lists are used to implement arrays.

teach.heading: Worked example: reading and changing a 2D array
teach.note: Model with the grid from the previous slide as scores = [[12,7,9],[5,14,3],[8,6,11]]. Insist on the order row, column. Afterwards ask a pupil what scores[2][0] is (8).

model.problem: scores is the 2D array in the table: row 0 is 12, 7, 9; row 1 is 5, 14, 3; row 2 is 8, 6, 11. State scores[1][2], then show the statement that changes the 14 to 20.
steps: Column 2 of that row is the third item, 3
model.answer: scores[1][2] is 3. The change is scores[1][1] = 20.

teach.heading: Check: array index
teach.note: Answer C. The index starts at 0, so the fourth item is index 3. A is the usual error (counting from 1). D tests whether pupils think the length is a valid index: with 5 items the last index is 4.

check.q: names = ['Sara', 'Bilal', 'Omar', 'Hana', 'Zayd']. Which statement outputs 'Hana'?
check.why: Hana is the fourth item, so its index is 3. names[4] is Zayd (A), names[2] is Omar (B) and names[5] is out of range (D).

practice: Give one advantage of using the constant PI = 3.14 rather than typing 3.14 each time.
Design a record for a library book with three fields, giving the data type of each.
grid = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]. State grid[1][0] and write the statement that sets the last item to 0.
independent: Core: A teacher stores five test scores in a 1D array. Write statements to read the third score and to change the first score to 18.
Extend: A 2D array holds the number of books borrowed on each day (columns) for three weeks (rows). Write code to output week 2, day 3 and the total for week 1.
Stretch: Explain when a record is a better choice than an array and when a 2D array is better. Use a school example for each.
exit: State one difference between a record and an array.
In a 2D array, which index comes first, the row or the column?
lessons.homework: Draw a 3 by 4 array holding a weekly prayer timetable of your choosing and write five statements that read or change cells.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a printed grid with numbered rows and columns and a word bank (row, column, index, field). Stretch: write a loop to total every cell of a 2D array.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.2: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
lessons.title: Operators and trace tables
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we find out what an algorithm does without running it?
objectives: Use arithmetic, relational and logical operators in algorithms (1.2.3)
Complete a trace table to work out outputs and variable values (1.2.4)
Describe what an algorithm does from its trace
successCriteria: All: evaluate expressions with arithmetic and relational operators
Most: complete a trace table for a loop
Some: use the trace to state the purpose of an unfamiliar algorithm
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: order of operations and iterative formulae
lessons.smsc: Moral: patience and accuracy (itqan) in checking each step

keywords.def: a symbol that carries out an operation on values
compares two values and gives True or False
combines conditions: AND, OR, NOT
a table that records the value of each variable as an algorithm runs

starter: Bismillah. Calculate 17 MOD 5 and 17 DIV 5.
What does the diamond in a flowchart do?
Name the three types of repetition or loop shown in the previous lesson.

teach.heading: Operators
bullets: Arithmetic: + - * / DIV MOD and powers
Relational: = != < > <= >=
Logical: AND, OR, NOT
teach.note: In Python DIV is // and MOD is %. Exam pseudocode may use either style; the paper always defines what it uses. Note that brackets and BIDMAS apply: * and / before + and -. Ask: what is 2 + 3 * 4? (14, not 20).

teach.heading: Trace table: record every change
bullets: One column per variable, plus output
Add a row each time a value changes
Follow the code exactly, do not guess
teach.note: Run the program with the class first without showing the output, then reveal it. Draw the trace table as pupils dictate. Point out that i is a variable too. The most common error is to skip the row where the loop condition fails.

teach.heading: Worked example: a while loop trace
teach.note: Model slowly, writing each row, and say the condition aloud each time. Ask pupils what the loop seems to calculate: it counts subtractions of 3, which is 8 DIV 3 plus one because the loop subtracts once more after n reaches 2. Stress that a trace tells you what the algorithm really does, which may differ from what you expected.

model.problem: Trace: n = 8, count = 0, WHILE n >= 0: n = n - 3, count = count + 1. Then OUTPUT count.
steps: Start: n = 8, count = 0. Condition 8 >= 0 is True
Row 3: n = -1, count = 3 (-1 >= 0 False, so the loop stops)
model.answer: The output is 3. The final n is -1. Note this is 8 DIV 3 plus one, because the loop subtracts once more after n reaches 2.

teach.heading: Answer: trace of the earlier program
teach.note: Pupils first complete their own trace of the program from the earlier slide, then you reveal this table. Only even values of i are added, so total goes 0, 2, 2, 6. Check they have a row for every pass of the loop.

teach.heading: Check: relational and logical operators
teach.note: Answer B. x > 3 is True, y < 10 is False, so True AND False is False; but the question uses OR. Work it through: x = 5, y = 12: x > 3 True; y < 10 False; OR gives True. Ask why option C (False) is the AND answer.

check.q: x = 5 and y = 12. What is the value of (x > 3) OR (y < 10)?
check.why: x > 3 is True. y < 10 is False. With OR, one True is enough, so the result is True. False would be the result of AND (A). The result of a relational test is a Boolean, not a number (C, D).

practice: Trace: a = 1, b = 1; repeat 4 times: c = a + b, a = b, b = c. Complete the table and give the final b.
State the purpose of this algorithm: SET s TO 0, FOR each digit d IN [4, 8, 1]: SET s TO s + d, OUTPUT s / 3.
independent: Core: Trace the program total = 1; for i in range(1, 4): total = total * 2; print(total). Show every row.
Extend: Write an algorithm using MOD to output 'even' or 'odd' for each number in [3, 10, 7, 12] and trace it.
Stretch: A trace of an unknown algorithm gives x: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. Describe the pattern, write the loop that produced it and state the next value.
exit: Calculate 29 MOD 6 and 29 DIV 6.
State why a trace table has a column for every variable.
lessons.homework: Write a short algorithm using a loop and one IF. Swap with a partner (or ask someone at home), trace it for the input 6 and write down what it does.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a pre-drawn trace table with column headings and the first row filled. Stretch: ask for the trace of a nested loop.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.2: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
lessons.title: Errors and test data: finding and fixing faults
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you prove a program works, and what do you do when it does not?
objectives: Identify syntax, logic and runtime errors (1.2.5)
Correct logic errors in an algorithm
Choose normal, boundary and erroneous test data and judge fitness for purpose (1.2.7)
successCriteria: All: name the three types of error and give an example of each
Most: spot and fix a logic error using a trace
Some: design a test plan with expected outcomes and judge whether a program is fit for purpose
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: fair testing and repeatable results
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty (sidq) in reporting that something is broken, rather than hiding it

keywords.def: code that breaks the rules of the language, so it cannot run
the program runs but gives wrong results because of faulty reasoning
an error that happens while the program is running and stops it
chosen inputs used to check a program, with the expected results
does the job it was designed for, correctly and efficiently

starter: Bismillah. What is a trace table used for?
Calculate 90 / 3 + 10 and 90 / (3 + 10) on paper, to 1 decimal place.
Why do we use meaningful variable names?

teach.heading: Three kinds of error
bullets: Syntax: rules broken, program will not start
Logic: runs, but the answer is wrong
Runtime: crashes while running
teach.note: Run all three programs on the next slides in turn if you have a computer. Ask pupils which type is hardest to find and why: logic errors give no error message. Emphasise that only the logic error needs a trace table to find.

head: Type
When detected
Example
rows: Before or as the program starts
Never by the computer; found by testing
Wrong operator or order of operations
Dividing by zero, index out of range

teach.heading: Syntax error
bullets: The translator reports the line
Fix: add the missing bracket
The program cannot run until fixed
teach.note: Read the message aloud and find the cause. In exams a syntax error is often a missing colon, bracket, quotation mark or misspelled keyword. Ask pupils to say how the translator helped them.

code.text: print("Salam"

teach.heading: Logic error
bullets: No error message appears
Output is 190.0, not the mean 90.0
Fix: brackets around the sum
teach.note: Pupils should calculate the correct mean first (60 + 90 + 120 = 270, divided by 3 is 90), then compare. The fault is the order of operations: division happens before addition. Show the fix: mean = (a + b + c) / 3. Link to the trace table: trace the faulty line to see where it diverges.

code.text:
a = 60
b = 90
c = 120
mean = a + b + c / 3
print(mean)

teach.heading: Worked example: find and fix
teach.note: Model the method: run with simple data you can predict, compare with the expected value, then trace to find the line. Point out that the logic error here is also an off-by-one, a very common exam error. The range stops before the second number.

model.problem: This code should output the sum of 1 to 5 (15) but outputs 10: total = 0; for i in range(1, 5): total = total + i; print(total). Find and fix the error.
steps: Trace: i takes 1, 2, 3, 4 only, so total is 10
model.answer: A logic error (off by one). The corrected loop is for i in range(1, 6), which outputs 15.

teach.heading: Runtime error and test data
bullets: Runtime: 10 / 0 stops the program
Normal data: typical valid values
Boundary data: the edges; erroneous data: invalid input
teach.note: Run the code to show the crash. Then introduce a test plan for a program that accepts ages from 11 to 16. Boundaries are both sides of each limit: 10, 11, 16, 17. Erroneous data includes the wrong type, such as 'abc'. Testing shows the presence of faults, not their absence.

code.text:
nums = [4, 0]
print(10 / nums[0])
print(10 / nums[1])

teach.heading: Check: type of error
teach.note: Answer C. The program runs and prints something, so it is not a syntax error; it does not crash, so it is not a runtime error; the result is wrong. Discuss why D is not an error type at all: bad style is not an error.

check.q: A program to find the area of a rectangle outputs 14 for width 3 and height 4, instead of 12. It runs without crashing. What type of error is this?
check.why: The program runs to the end but the result is wrong, so the logic is faulty (it added 3 + 4 instead of multiplying). A syntax error stops the program starting (A); a runtime error crashes it (B).

practice: Classify each fault: (a) a missing colon after if; (b) a program that adds VAT twice; (c) asking for list[10] in a list of 5 items.
A program accepts exam marks from 0 to 100. Give one normal, two boundary and one erroneous test value for the valid range.
Explain how a trace table helps find a logic error.
independent: Core: Fix the error and state its type: for i in range(3) print(i).
Extend: Write a test plan table (input, type of data, expected result) for a program that accepts a password of 8 to 12 characters.
Stretch: A program to find the largest of three numbers always outputs the first number. Describe how you would test it, what data you would choose and how you would find the line at fault.
exit: Name the three types of error. Which one does the computer never report?
Give one example of boundary data for a program that accepts numbers from 1 to 50.
lessons.homework: Write a short program in Python containing one syntax, one logic and one runtime error (in three separate versions). Annotate each with the type and the fix.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sorting task with the three error types as cards and example snippets. Stretch: ask for a test plan with 8 rows covering every kind of test data.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.2: Computational thinking: algorithms, data structures and testing
lessons.title: Efficiency of searches and sorts
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we decide which algorithm is better when they all give the right answer?
objectives: Explain how bubble sort, merge sort, linear search and binary search work (1.2.6)
Compare algorithms by counting passes and comparisons (1.2.7)
Choose a suitable algorithm for a given situation
successCriteria: All: describe each algorithm in one sentence
Most: carry out a merge sort and count binary search checks
Some: justify an algorithm choice by comparing the number of comparisons as the list grows
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: powers of 2 and halving
lessons.smsc: Moral: ihsan (excellence) in choosing the best method, not just the first one

keywords.def: how little time or memory an algorithm needs for a job
checking two values against each other
one complete run through the list in a sort
arranged in a given order, such as ascending

starter: Bismillah. Why must a list be sorted before a binary search?
Sort 4, 9, 2 using bubble sort and show the list after the first pass.
Write the middle item of 2, 5, 8, 11, 14.

teach.heading: Bubble sort in code
bullets: Compare neighbours, swap if out of order
Repeat passes until a pass has no swaps
Output shows the list after each pass
teach.note: Pupils have met bubble sort in lesson 5 of the existing unit; here we trace the code and count passes. Point out the swapped flag: it lets the algorithm stop early. Ask how many passes an already sorted list needs (one, to confirm no swaps).

code.text:
data = [5, 3, 8, 1]
passes = 0
swapped = True
while swapped:
    swapped = False
    for i in range(len(data) - 1):
        if data[i] > data[i + 1]:
            data[i], data[i + 1] = data[i + 1], data[i]
            swapped = True
    passes = passes + 1
    print(passes, data)

teach.heading: Binary search in code
bullets: Check the middle item each time
Discard half the list after every check
Count the checks to compare efficiency
teach.note: Trace the code with the whole class, drawing low, mid and high. The list is sorted, which is essential. Compare: a linear search would take 6 checks to reach 27, binary took fewer. Pupils should state the result in words using 'checks'.

code.text:
nums = [3, 8, 12, 15, 21, 27, 34, 40, 52]
target = 27
low = 0
high = len(nums) - 1
checks = 0
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) // 2
    checks = checks + 1
    if nums[mid] == target:
        print("found at", mid, "after", checks, "checks")
        break
    elif nums[mid] < target:
        low = mid + 1
    else:
        high = mid - 1

teach.heading: How the work grows
bullets: Linear search: up to n checks
Binary search: halves each time, about log2 n
Merge sort splits then merges; bubble sort needs many passes
teach.note: Let pupils notice that doubling the list adds only one extra check for binary search. This is the key idea for 'efficiency' answers. Merge sort needs extra memory for the merged lists; bubble sort sorts in place. Do not ask for formulae beyond this table.

teach.heading: Worked example: merge sort
teach.note: Model on the board in two colours: splits in one, merges in another. Emphasise that in the merge step the first items of each list are compared and the smaller is moved. Say the stages aloud: split, split, merge, merge. Link to the cost: the extra lists use more memory.

model.problem: Use a merge sort on 7, 2, 9, 4. Show every stage.
steps: Merge the two lists: compare 2 and 4 (take 2), 7 and 4 (take 4), 7 and 9 (take 7), then 9
model.answer: The sorted list is [2, 4, 7, 9].

teach.heading: Check: choosing an algorithm
teach.note: Answer B. The list is unsorted, so binary search would give wrong results (D, the trap). Sorting first just to search once is slow for a single lookup. Ask why the answer would change if the contacts list was searched thousands of times.

check.q: A teacher has an unsorted list of 40 names and wants to find one name once. Which is the best choice?
options: Binary search on the list as it is
check.why: With one search on an unsorted list, a linear search needs at most 40 checks and no sorting. Binary search only works on a sorted list (D), and sorting first (A, C) costs extra work for a single lookup.

practice: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of merge sort compared with bubble sort.
Write the first pass of a bubble sort on [6, 2, 9, 1].
A sorted list has 16 items. State the most checks a binary search could need (hint: halve 16 repeatedly to 1).
independent: Core: Carry out a merge sort on 5, 1, 4, 8, 2, 7, 3, 6, showing every split and merge.
Extend: Trace the binary search code for target = 8 in the same list and give the number of checks.
Stretch: A website sorts 1 000 000 prices once and then answers many searches. Explain, using the number of checks, why sorting first is worth it.
exit: Why is binary search faster than linear search on a large sorted list?
State one fact that makes merge sort better than bubble sort for large lists.
lessons.homework: Write a half-page comparing linear and binary search using a library catalogue as the example. Include the checks needed for 1000 books.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give cut-up cards of a merge sort to rearrange into order. Stretch: ask for the most checks for 1000 items and the reasoning. Existing y10 lessons 4 to 6 teach how the algorithms work; this lesson adds code tracing and efficiency comparison.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.3: Computational thinking: logic and truth tables
lessons.title: Logic gates and truth tables: AND, OR and NOT
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a computer decide yes or no from several pieces of information?
objectives: Complete truth tables for AND, OR and NOT (1.3.1)
Write and read logic expressions with up to two inputs
Relate logic expressions to conditions in programs
successCriteria: All: complete the truth tables for AND, OR and NOT
Most: complete a truth table for a combined two-input expression
Some: write an expression from a description and show two expressions are not the same
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: Venn diagrams and set logic (AND is intersection, OR is union)
lessons.smsc: Moral: sound judgement uses all the evidence, as logic combines inputs fairly

keywords.def: a value that is either True or False (1 or 0)
output is True only if both inputs are True
output is True if at least one input is True
reverses the input: True becomes False
lists every combination of inputs and the output for each

starter: Bismillah. What is the output of 5 > 3 in Python?
Name the data type that holds True or False.
How many different combinations of two inputs, each 0 or 1, are there?

teach.heading: The three operators
bullets: AND: both must be 1
OR: at least one is 1
NOT: flips the value
teach.note: Link to real life: you can enter the exam hall if you have a pen AND your ID. Rows in a truth table go in counting order, 00, 01, 10, 11. Say that the same rules apply in Python with and, or and not. Pupils often confuse OR with 'exactly one': in computing OR includes both.

teach.heading: Same thing in Python
bullets: Booleans are True and False
and, or, not work on them
Loop through every combination
teach.note: Run the program: the output columns mirror the table (with True and False instead of 1 and 0). Ask pupils to match each column to the table. This shows that a truth table is just a record of every possible input.

code.output:
False False False False True
False True False True True
True False False True False
True True True True False

teach.heading: Worked example: a combined expression
teach.note: Model by working out the middle column first: the bracket is evaluated before the final operator. Build the table row by row. Emphasise writing the intermediate column; marks are often given for it.

model.problem: Complete the truth table for the expression A OR (NOT B).
steps: Four rows for the inputs A and B: 00, 01, 10, 11
Combine with A using OR: row 00 -> 0 OR 1 = 1; row 01 -> 0 OR 0 = 0
model.answer: Output column: 1, 0, 1, 1.

teach.heading: Misconception: NOT over brackets
bullets: NOT (A AND B) gives 1, 1, 1, 0
NOT A AND NOT B gives 1, 0, 0, 0
The expressions are different
teach.note: Ask pupils to build both columns to prove it. The brackets matter: NOT applies to the whole bracket. This is useful when writing conditions such as not (a and b).

misconception.wrong: NOT (A AND B) is the same as (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
misconception.right: They are different. NOT (A AND B) is 1 unless both inputs are 1; (NOT A) AND (NOT B) is 1 only when both are 0.

teach.heading: Check: AND or OR?
teach.note: Answer D. 'Either' here means at least one, which is OR; then the output is 1 for rows with a 1 in A or B. Option A is the AND column. Ask how the table would change if the rule were: A AND NOT B.

check.q: A garden light switches on if the sensor detects movement (A) or the manual switch is on (B). For A = 1 and B = 0, what is the output?
check.why: The rule is OR, so one input at 1 is enough. The AND rule would give 0 (A, B). NOT A is not part of the rule (C).

practice: Complete the truth table for NOT A AND B (inputs A and B).
Write a Python condition that is True if age >= 11 and age <= 16.
Write the logic expression: a door alarm sounds if the door is open (D) AND the system is armed (S).
independent: Core: Complete the truth tables for A AND B, A OR B and NOT (A OR B).
Extend: Write a logic expression and truth table for: a school gate stays locked if it is after 4 pm (P) OR the key is not in the office (K).
Stretch: Show, using truth tables, that NOT (A OR B) is the same as (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
exit: Complete: 1 AND 0 = ?, 1 OR 0 = ?, NOT 1 = ?
Write the Python form of the expression 'A OR NOT B'.
lessons.homework: Find two real conditions from home or the masjid (for example 'open if it is Friday and before 2 pm') and write each as a logic expression with a truth table.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a blank truth table with the inputs filled in and a key (1 = true). Stretch: ask for expressions with a hidden NOT and justify the output.

lessons.unit: Unit 1.3: Computational thinking: logic and truth tables
lessons.title: Three-input logic and conditions in programs
lessons.bigQuestion: How do real systems combine three or more conditions?
objectives: Complete truth tables with three inputs (1.3.1)
Write logic expressions from a description and read them back
Relate expressions to conditions in Python programs
successCriteria: All: list all eight combinations of three inputs
Most: complete a three-input truth table for a bracketed expression
Some: write an expression from a scenario and use the truth table to test a program condition
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: control systems with several sensors
lessons.smsc: Moral: caution and care (taqwa in action): safety systems must consider every case

keywords.def: a value fed into a logic expression
a combination of inputs and operators, such as (A AND B) OR C
groups part of an expression to be worked out first
a Boolean test in a program, such as age > 16

starter: Bismillah. Write the truth table for A OR B.
What is the value of NOT (1 AND 0)?
Write a Python condition for 'x is between 1 and 9'.

teach.heading: Eight rows
bullets: Three inputs give 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 rows
Write rows in counting order, 000 to 111
Work out brackets in a helper column
teach.note: Show the pattern: C alternates every row, B every two, A every four. Ask what four inputs would need (16 rows). Pupils lose marks by missing rows or writing them out of order.

teach.heading: From scenario to expression
bullets: Underline the words AND, OR, NOT
Give each condition a letter
Use brackets to match the meaning
teach.note: Work through: an alarm sounds if the door is open and it is night or the owner is away. Pupils must decide where the bracket goes; 'open AND (night OR away)'. Compare with (open AND night) OR away and ask when they differ.

code.text:
door_open = True
night = False
away = True
alarm = door_open and (night or away)
print(alarm)
alarm2 = (door_open and night) or away
print(alarm2)
door_open = False
print(door_open and (night or away))

teach.heading: Worked example: three-input table
teach.note: Model using a helper column for the bracket B OR C first. Remind pupils that NOT A AND (B OR C) is only 1 when A is 0 and at least one of B, C is 1. Let pupils check the table by reading out the rows that equal 1: there are three.

model.problem: Complete the truth table for NOT A AND (B OR C).
steps: List the eight rows from 000 to 111
AND the two columns together row by row
model.answer: Output column: 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0.

teach.heading: Check: reading an expression
teach.note: Answer A. Rows where A = 1 and B = 1 give 1 for A AND B regardless of C. The only row for which the bracketed expression is 1 with C = 0 is 110. Option C is the trap of reading the expression as A OR B.

check.q: Which input row gives an output of 1 for the expression (A AND B) AND NOT C?
check.why: Both A and B must be 1 and C must be 0 so that NOT C is 1. The other rows each break one of those three requirements.

practice: Complete the truth table for (A OR B) AND C.
Write an expression for: a heater runs if it is cold (C) and the window is closed (W) or the override switch (O) is on.
Write the Python statement that stores the result of the expression in the previous question in the variable heater_on.
independent: Core: Complete the truth table for A AND (NOT B) AND C.

Extend: A lift moves only if the door is closed (D), the lift is not overloaded (O) and a button is pressed (B). Write the expression, build the table and state in how many of the eight rows the lift moves.
Stretch: Write a Python function with three Boolean parameters that returns True only if exactly one of them is True. Give its truth table.
exit: How many rows has a truth table with three inputs?
Write the expression 'A or B, and C' with brackets correctly placed.
lessons.homework: Choose a safety system (a car seatbelt warning, an oven door lock). Write its logic as an expression with three inputs and a truth table.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a pre-filled template with the eight input rows and the helper column labelled. Stretch: show the expression can be rewritten without brackets and test it with a truth table.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.1: Data: binary and number representation
lessons.title: Bits, states and unsigned binary
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a computer store anything at all using only on and off?
objectives: Explain that binary represents data and instructions and count the states for n bits (2.1.1)
Convert between denary and 8-bit unsigned binary, 0 to 255 (2.1.2, 2.1.3)
State the largest value for a given number of bits
successCriteria: All: convert a small denary number to binary and back
Most: convert any value 0 to 255 in both directions
Some: work out the number of bits needed for a given number of values and justify it
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: powers of 2 and place value
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the idea of simple, reliable building blocks combining into something vast

keywords.def: a binary digit, 0 or 1
8 bits
base 10, the number system we normally use
base 2, using only the digits 0 and 1
one possible pattern of a group of bits

starter: Bismillah. Write the first eight powers of 2 (1, 2, 4 ...).
What is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2?
Convert 13 into a sum of 8, 4, 2 and 1 (for example 13 = 8 + 4 + 1).

teach.heading: Why binary?
bullets: Computers use switches that are on or off
Data and instructions are both stored as bits
A bit is 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits
teach.note: Explain that circuits are made of transistors with two reliable states; two states are easy to tell apart and resist noise. Stress that program instructions are stored as binary just as data is; the computer cannot tell which it is without context. Ask pupils what a pattern like 01000001 could mean (the number 65 or the letter A).

teach.heading: Place values
bullets: Each place is double the place on its right
Largest 8-bit value is 255, not 256
teach.note: Draw the place-value headings on the board and keep them there all lesson. Note that 8 bits give 256 states but the values run from 0 to 255 because 0 is a state. Pupils often write 256 as the maximum.

teach.heading: Worked example: denary to binary
teach.note: Model by subtracting place values from the left: if the place value fits, write 1 and subtract; if not, write 0. Check by adding the place values back. Say the check aloud so pupils see it as part of the method.

model.problem: Convert 77 to 8-bit binary.
model.answer: 77 in binary is 01001101.

teach.heading: Binary to denary, and the checker
bullets: Add the place values where there is a 1
Python can check your working
teach.note: Pupils should work out 10110010 first. Python's int(text, 2) and format() are only for checking; in the exam, conversions are done by hand. Ask why the leading zero in 01001101 must be kept when we say '8-bit'.

teach.heading: Check: how many values?
teach.note: Answer C. With n bits there are 2^n states: 2^6 = 64. A doubles instead of using the power. B is 6 x 6; D confuses the number of states with the largest value (63).

check.q: A sensor sends a 6-bit binary pattern. How many different patterns can it send?
check.why: 6 bits give 2^6 = 64 patterns (0 to 63). 12 is 6 x 2 (A), 36 is 6 x 6 (B) and 63 is the largest value, not the number of patterns (D).

practice: Convert 45 to 8-bit binary and show a check.
Convert 11001001 to denary.
How many bits are needed to give a different pattern to each of 100 pupils? Explain.
independent: Core: Convert 19, 100 and 255 to 8-bit binary.
Extend: Convert 01101110, 10000001 and 11111110 to denary, and state the largest number that can be stored in 10 bits.
Stretch: A game has 300 different items. Work out the minimum number of bits to give each item its own code and say how many spare codes there are.
exit: State the number of values that 5 bits can represent.
Convert 00010110 to denary.
lessons.homework: Write your age, your house number and the number of letters in your name in 8-bit binary. Show working for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: keep the place-value strip visible and provide a template with the 8 columns. Stretch: ask for conversions using 12-bit binary and the number of states.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.1: Data: binary and number representation
lessons.title: Signed integers and two's complement
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a computer store negative numbers using only 0s and 1s?
objectives: Represent signed integers using two's complement (2.1.2)
Convert between denary and 8-bit two's complement, -128 to +127 (2.1.3)
Explain the range of signed and unsigned 8-bit integers
successCriteria: All: state the range of 8-bit signed integers
Most: convert positive and negative numbers in both directions
Some: explain why two's complement is useful and spot an invalid conversion
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: negative numbers and number lines
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness in treating negative values as seriously as positive ones

keywords.def: a binary number with no sign: all bits are used for the value
a binary number that can be positive or negative
a way of storing signed numbers where the leftmost bit has a negative place value
the leftmost bit, with the largest place value

starter: Bismillah. Convert 52 to 8-bit binary.
What is the largest unsigned 8-bit value?
What is -128 + 64?

teach.heading: The idea
bullets: Leftmost bit has a negative value: -128
Other bits keep their positive values
Range is -128 to +127
teach.note: The idea is the same place-value method with one change. Show that with a leading 1 the number starts at -128 and the other bits add back. The number is negative if and only if the leading bit is 1. Compare unsigned 255 with signed -1 for the same pattern.

teach.heading: Binary to denary
bullets: Place values: -128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1
teach.note: Work through the sum aloud: 64 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 118, and -128 + 118 = -10. Point out that a leading 1 means the answer is at most -1. Pupils like to ignore the first bit and read the rest; correct that now.

teach.heading: Worked example: negative to binary
teach.note: Model the method of 'write the positive number, flip the bits, add 1'. Then check using the place values. Both methods lead to the same answer; pupils may use either as long as they check. Emphasise that the number of bits must be fixed at 8 so the leading zeros matter.

model.problem: Write -45 as an 8-bit two's complement number.

teach.heading: Misconception: sign and magnitude
bullets: Not just a minus sign bit
The leading bit is worth -128
teach.note: Pupils often think the leading 1 just means 'negative' and the rest is the size. Test it: -128 + 4 + 1 = -123. Sign-and-magnitude is a different system and is not the one used in this course.

misconception.wrong: In 8-bit two's complement, 10000101 is -5 (a minus sign then 0000101).
misconception.right: The leading bit is worth -128, so 10000101 = -128 + 4 + 1 = -123.

teach.heading: Check: convert
teach.note: Answer B. The leading 1 means the number is negative: -128 + 64 + 8 + 4 + 2 = -50. Option A is the unsigned value, 206. C comes from reading the other seven bits as 78 and just adding a minus sign. D has the right size but the wrong sign.

check.q: What is 11001110 as an 8-bit two's complement number?
check.why: -128 + 64 + 8 + 4 + 2 = -50. The unsigned value is 206 (A). C wrongly treats the leading 1 as just a minus sign in front of 78; 50 has the wrong sign (D).

practice: State the smallest and largest 8-bit two's complement integers.
Write -1 and -128 in 8-bit two's complement.
Convert 10100000 to denary.
independent: Core: Convert 00111100 and 11000100 to denary (two's complement).
Extend: Write -20, -75 and 99 in 8-bit two's complement.
Stretch: Explain why the range is -128 to +127 and not -127 to +128, using the number of patterns available for positive numbers, zero and negative numbers.
exit: Write -3 in 8-bit two's complement.
What is the smallest number that 8-bit two's complement can store?
lessons.homework: Make a conversion chart for the numbers -8 to +7 in 4-bit two's complement (place values -8, 4, 2, 1).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a place-value strip with -128 in a different colour. Stretch: ask for 16-bit extreme values (-32 768 to +32 767) with reasoning.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.1: Data: binary and number representation
lessons.title: Binary addition, shifts and overflow
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens when a calculation produces a number too big for the bits available?
objectives: Add positive binary numbers (2.1.4)
Apply logical and arithmetic shifts and state their effect (2.1.4)
Explain overflow when a result exceeds the available bits (2.1.5)
successCriteria: All: add two small binary numbers using carries
Most: shift a pattern left or right and give the effect on its value
Some: identify overflow, give the stored result and explain the consequence
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: multiplying and dividing by powers of 2
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty about the limits of a system, reporting an error instead of hiding it

keywords.def: the 1 moved to the next column when a column adds to more than 1
moves all bits left or right and fills the gap with 0
a shift that keeps the sign bit, so signed numbers keep their sign
a result too large for the number of bits available

starter: Bismillah. Convert 00011010 to denary.
How many different values can 8 bits hold?
What is 6 x 2 and 6 x 4?

teach.heading: Adding binary
bullets: 1+1+1=11 (write 1, carry 1)
Work from the right, column by column
teach.note: Practise the four rules orally before any sums. Pupils must write the carries above the next column. Most errors come from forgetting the carry into a column with two 1s. Remind pupils that after adding they should convert to denary to check.

teach.heading: Worked example: add two bytes
teach.note: Model column by column from the right with the carry written above. After finishing, convert both inputs and the answer to denary: 53 + 27 = 80. This builds the habit of checking.

model.problem: Add 00110101 and 00011011, giving the answer in 8 bits.
steps: Next: 1 + 0 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1. Next: 0 + 1 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1
Next: 1 + 1 + 1 = 11, write 1, carry 1. Next: 1 + 0 + 1 = 10, write 0, carry 1. Then 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, and 0 + 0 = 0

teach.heading: Shifts
bullets: Left shift by 1 doubles the value
Right shift by 1 halves it, losing a remainder
Arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit
teach.note: Show the Python output as confirmation: shifting left by 1 gives 44 (22 x 2) and shifting right by 2 gives 5 (22 divided by 4, remainder lost). The last line shifts 11 left by 3 places to give 88, a multiplication by 8. For a logical shift, the vacated bits are filled with zeros. For an arithmetic right shift on a signed number the sign bit is copied so that a negative number stays negative: 11110100 (-12) becomes 11111010 (-6). A logical right shift would give 01111010, which is 122 and wrong. Pupils should always state the effect as multiplying or dividing by a power of 2.

code.text:
a = 22
print(format(a << 1, "08b"), a << 1)
print(format(a >> 2, "08b"), a >> 2)
print(format(11, "08b"), format((11 << 3) % 256, "08b"))

teach.heading: Overflow
bullets: The result needs more than 8 bits
The extra bit is lost, so the stored value is wrong
Example: 150 + 110 = 260, stored as 4
teach.note: Run the code. Python integers are unbounded, so we simulate an 8-bit register with % 256. Consequences: wrong results, crashes or security holes. Emphasise that overflow is about the fixed number of bits, not about the computer being slow or broken.

code.text:
total = 150 + 110
print(total)
print(total % 256)
print(format(total % 256, "08b"))

teach.heading: Check: shifts
teach.note: Answer D. A left shift of 2 multiplies by 4: 12 x 4 = 48 = 00110000. A is a right shift. B moves only one place. C is 00001100 shifted the wrong way and read incorrectly. Ask what would happen to 11000000 shifted left by 1: a 1 falls off the end, a logical overflow.

check.q: The 8-bit pattern 00001100 (12) is shifted left by two places. What is the new value?
check.why: Each left shift doubles the value: 12 x 2 x 2 = 48 (00110000). A is a right shift by 2, B is a shift by one place, and C is unchanged.

practice: Add 00101101 and 00010110 and check in denary.
Shift 00010100 right by 2 and state the denary value before and after.
Add 11001000 and 01100100. Is there overflow? State the stored 8-bit result.
independent: Core: Add 01000111 and 00101010; convert all three to denary to check.
Extend: A byte holds 00000110. Show the effect of left shifts by 1, 2 and 3 and relate each to multiplication.
