Stretch: Explain why a logical right shift gives the wrong answer for a negative two's complement number and how an arithmetic shift fixes it, using -16 as the example.
exit: What does a left shift of 3 places do to the value (if no 1 falls off)?
Define overflow in your own words and give one effect.
lessons.homework: Make a table of every addition from 100 + 100 to 100 + 160 (in steps of 20) and mark which ones overflow an 8-bit unsigned register.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a column-addition template with carry boxes. Stretch: ask for an arithmetic shift of a negative number.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.1: Data: binary and number representation
lessons.title: Hexadecimal
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do programmers write 'FF' when the computer stores 11111111?
objectives: Explain why hexadecimal is used (2.1.6)
Convert between hexadecimal and binary
Convert between hexadecimal and denary
successCriteria: All: state two reasons for using hexadecimal
Most: convert between binary and hex using nibbles
Some: convert denary to hex and justify use of hex in a given context
lessons.crossCurricular: Art and Design: web colour codes
lessons.smsc: Cultural: people create notation that is easier for humans to read

keywords.def: base 16, using digits 0 to 9 and letters A to F
4 bits, which is one hexadecimal digit
the number of different digits a number system uses

starter: Bismillah. Convert 11010110 to denary.
How many values can 4 bits hold?
What is 12 x 16?

teach.heading: Why hex?
bullets: Shorter: one hex digit for 4 bits
Easier to read, write and remember
Easier to spot mistakes than a string of 1s and 0s
teach.note: Show a long binary string and its hex form side by side. Hexadecimal does not make computers faster; it is for people. Real uses: web colours, MAC addresses, memory addresses, error codes. Ask pupils why 'F' appears (15 needs one digit).

teach.heading: Binary to hex and back
bullets: Split into nibbles from the right
Convert each nibble to one hex digit
Reverse the steps to go from hex to binary
teach.note: Model 10111100: nibbles 1011 and 1100, which are B and C, so BC. Practise reading the table the other way. Stress writing out four bits for each digit, including leading zeros: hex 3 is 0011, not 11.

code.text:
print(format(0b10111100, "X"))
print(format(0xC3, "08b"))
print(int("C3", 16))

teach.heading: Worked example: hex to denary and denary to hex
teach.note: Model both directions and the check. For hex to denary: first digit x 16 plus second digit. For denary to hex: divide by 16; the quotient is the first digit and the remainder is the second. Pupils must remember that C is 12, not 3.

model.problem: (a) Convert 3A to binary and denary. (b) Convert denary 200 to hex.
steps: 12 is C, remainder 8, so the hex is C8 (check: 12 x 16 + 8 = 200)

teach.heading: Misconception: adding the digits of FF
bullets: A to F stand for 10 to 15
FF is 255, not 30
Hex digits are worth 16s, not 10s
teach.note: Pupils add F + F as 15 + 15 = 30. Show that FF = 15 x 16 + 15 = 255, the biggest byte. Link to the colour code #FF0000 (maximum red, no green or blue).

misconception.wrong: FF in hexadecimal is 30, because F + F = 15 + 15.
misconception.right: FF = 15 x 16 + 15 = 255. The first digit is worth 16 times its value.

teach.heading: Check: bits in hex
teach.note: Answer A. Each hex digit stands for 4 bits so 2 digits stand for 8 bits, one byte. B would be 16 bits, 4 digits. C and D confuse digits and bits.

check.q: How many bits are represented by the hexadecimal number 7F?
check.why: Each hex digit represents a nibble of 4 bits, so two digits represent 8 bits. 4 bits is one digit (B), 2 is the number of digits (C) and 16 bits would need 4 digits (D).

practice: Convert 11100101 to hexadecimal.
Convert 9D to 8-bit binary and to denary.
State two reasons for using hexadecimal rather than binary when displaying memory addresses.
independent: Core: Convert 00101111, 11111110 and 10010001 to hexadecimal.
Extend: Convert 6B, F0 and A5 to denary; convert 100 and 255 to hexadecimal.
Stretch: The web colour #1E90FF has red 1E, green 90 and blue FF. Convert each part to denary and describe the colour in terms of how much of each primary there is.
exit: Write 15 and 16 in hexadecimal.
Explain in one sentence why hex is more convenient than binary for humans.
lessons.homework: Find the hex colour codes of three colours used on a website you know. Convert each of the red, green and blue values to denary.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give the table of 16 hex digits with binary as a reference card. Stretch: ask for a three-byte colour value to be written in binary.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.2: Data: representing text, images and sound
lessons.title: Representing text: ASCII and the limits of fixed bits
lessons.bigQuestion: If every letter is a number, what happens when the alphabet does not fit?
objectives: Represent characters using 7-bit ASCII (2.2.1)
Work out the code for a character from its position in the alphabet
Explain the limits of binary representation when the number of bits is fixed (2.2.4)
successCriteria: All: state how many characters 7-bit ASCII can represent
Most: find the ASCII code of a letter or word given one reference code
Some: explain how a fixed number of bits limits characters, numbers and quality
lessons.crossCurricular: Arabic and RE: why writing systems such as Arabic needed more than ASCII
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and cultural: digital respect for the Arabic script; the Qur'an and other texts can be stored accurately using Unicode, which goes beyond ASCII

keywords.def: the list of characters a computer can represent and the code for each
a 7-bit character set with 128 codes
the number given to a character
the system uses the same number of bits each time, which limits what it can store

starter: Bismillah. How many patterns can 7 bits give?
Convert 65 to binary.
What does the letter H have as the next letter in the alphabet?

teach.heading: ASCII
bullets: Each character has a 7-bit code
128 characters: letters, digits, punctuation, control codes
Capital letters, small letters and digits are in order
teach.note: Show the table. The codes are consecutive, so you can work out C from A. Note: capital A is 65 and small a is 97, a gap of 32; the digit '0' is code 48, not zero. Pupils often confuse the character '5' with the number 5.

teach.heading: Working with codes
bullets: Count along the alphabet from a known code
ord gives the code, chr gives the character
Each letter is stored in one 7-bit pattern
teach.note: Run the code and compare with the table. Pupils see that D is A + 3 and that the codes are stored as binary. Ask what 'Salam' looks like in memory (five 7-bit patterns). Point out that Python uses its own larger character set but the first 128 codes are the same.

code.text:
word = "Salam"
for ch in word:
    print(ch, ord(ch), format(ord(ch), "07b"))
print(chr(ord("A") + 3))

teach.heading: Worked example: encode a word
teach.note: Model step by step: use the reference code and count. Then convert to 7-bit binary using place values 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. Check each against a known reference such as 'A is 1000001'. Ask what the code for 'i' would be if you only knew that 'a' is 97 (97 + 8 = 105).

model.problem: Given that A is 65, write the ASCII codes for the letters D and H in denary and 7-bit binary.

teach.heading: Limits of a fixed number of bits
bullets: 7 bits: only 128 characters, mostly English
Arabic letters and emoji do not fit in ASCII
8 bits: 0 to 255 only; 8-bit images: 256 colours
teach.note: Draw the general rule: n bits give 2^n values, so a fixed n always has a limit. More bits means a wider range or more detail but more storage. Unicode is a larger character set that uses more bits and includes Arabic and many other scripts; knowing the name is useful, but the exam asks for the limits idea. Link to overflow and sound quality.

teach.heading: Check: how many?
teach.note: Answer B. 7 bits give 2^7 = 128 different codes. C is the 8-bit count. D is the largest 7-bit value. Link to the limit idea: the number of characters is fixed by the number of bits.

check.q: How many different characters can 7-bit ASCII represent?
check.why: 2^7 = 128 codes (0 to 127). 256 would need 8 bits (C), 64 is 6 bits (A), and 127 is the largest code, not the number of characters (D).

practice: Given that a is 97, write the ASCII codes for c and f in denary.
Convert the word 'Hi' (H = 72, i = 105) into 7-bit binary.
Explain one limit of ASCII for a school with pupils who write in Arabic.
independent: Core: Using A = 65, write the denary codes for the letters of 'FAITH' and the 7-bit binary for the first letter.
Extend: A text file has 250 characters in 7-bit ASCII. Calculate the number of bits and bytes needed.
Stretch: A system stores each character in 6 bits. State how many characters it can represent and what could go wrong if a new character is added.
exit: State the number of ASCII characters and the number of bits for each.
Give one limit of using a fixed number of bits.
lessons.homework: Write your first name and your mother's name in ASCII denary codes, with a short note on any characters that could not be shown.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the ASCII reference table with codes for A, a and 0 marked. Stretch: build a short substitution cipher with chr and ord.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.2: Data: representing text, images and sound
lessons.title: Representing images and sound
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a picture or a voice be turned into numbers and rebuilt later?
objectives: Describe bitmap images using pixels, resolution and colour depth (2.2.2)
Describe sound sampling using amplitude, sample rate, bit depth and sample interval (2.2.3)
Explain how changing these properties changes quality and file size
successCriteria: All: define pixel, resolution and colour depth
Most: calculate the number of colours and the sample interval
Some: explain the trade-off between quality and file size for both images and sound
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: waves, amplitude and frequency
lessons.smsc: Cultural: recording a recitation faithfully (amanah) so that it can be heard again clearly

keywords.def: the smallest single dot of colour in a bitmap image
the number of pixels in the image (width x height)
the number of bits used for each pixel
the number of sound samples taken each second, in hertz
the number of bits used for each sound sample
the time between samples, equal to 1 divided by the sample rate
the height of a sound wave, which sets how loud it is

starter: Bismillah. How many colours can 3 bits represent?
Convert 10100 to denary.
Convert 2 minutes into seconds.

teach.heading: Bitmap images
bullets: The image is a grid of pixels
Each pixel stores a binary colour code
Resolution = width x height of the grid
teach.note: Show the 5 x 5 grid for the letter T. 1 means black and 0 means white, so one bit per pixel. Each row can be read out as a binary number. Pupils should write each row as binary. In exams, they must state that the image is stored as binary values for each pixel.

teach.heading: Colour depth
bullets: More bits per pixel means more colours
Colours = 2 to the power of the colour depth
More pixels or more depth means a bigger file
teach.note: Run the code. Show the colours doubling with each extra bit. 24-bit colour uses 8 bits each for red, green and blue. Link to hexadecimal colour codes from the previous lesson if pupils have studied it.

code.text:
for depth in (1, 2, 8, 24):
    print(depth, "bit:", 2 ** depth, "colours")
code.output:
1 bit: 2 colours
2 bit: 4 colours
8 bit: 256 colours
24 bit: 16777216 colours

teach.heading: Sound sampling
bullets: Analogue sound is a continuous wave
Measure the amplitude at regular intervals
Each measurement is stored as a binary number
teach.note: Draw a wave and mark equal vertical lines: each is one sample. The sample rate in Hz is samples per second, and the interval is the gap between them. A higher sample rate or bit depth gives a closer copy but a larger file. Pupils confuse sample rate with bit depth: rate is how often, depth is how precisely.

code.text:
rate = 8000
print("interval:", 1 / rate, "seconds")
print("levels with 8 bits:", 2 ** 8)
print("levels with 16 bits:", 2 ** 16)
code.output:
interval: 0.000125 seconds
levels with 8 bits: 256
levels with 16 bits: 65536

teach.heading: Worked example: image and sound properties
teach.note: Model with a calculation of the colours first, then the stored size in bits and bytes. Link to the next unit on file sizes. Sound: the interval is the reciprocal of the sample rate. Make the point that both the resolution and the depth are chosen by the designer, balancing quality against file size.

model.problem: An image is 16 pixels wide and 16 pixels high with a colour depth of 4 bits. State the number of colours and the data needed for the image in bits and bytes.
model.answer: 16 colours; 1024 bits, which is 128 bytes.

teach.heading: Check: effect of changing a property
teach.note: Answer C. Doubling both width and height gives four times as many pixels, so four times the data. A is the double-width only. D forgets that file size follows from the number of pixels. Ask: what would doubling just the colour depth do?

check.q: A bitmap's width and height are both doubled. The colour depth stays the same. What happens to the file size (before any compression)?
check.why: Doubling both width and height gives 2 x 2 = 4 times as many pixels, so 4 times the data. Doubling only one dimension would double it (A).

practice: A 1-bit image has 8 x 8 pixels. How many bits does it need and how many colours can it show?
State the sample interval for a sample rate of 4000 Hz.
Explain two ways to make a recording of a recitation sound closer to the original.
independent: Core: A 32 x 32 image uses 8-bit colour depth. State the number of colours and the number of bytes needed.
Extend: Compare a sound recorded at 8000 Hz, 8 bits with one at 16 000 Hz, 16 bits. Explain the effect on quality and on file size.
Stretch: A designer wants to halve the file size of an image without changing its resolution. State what could be changed and what the cost would be.
exit: Define colour depth.
What does a higher sample rate do to the sound and the file size?
lessons.homework: Make a 6 x 6 pixel image of a simple shape as a grid of 0s and 1s and write the binary for each row.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a ready-drawn 5 x 5 grid and a labelled diagram of a sampled wave. Stretch: ask for the quality-size trade-off to be evaluated.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.3: Data: storage units and compression
lessons.title: Storage units and file sizes
lessons.bigQuestion: How big is a file, and will it fit on the device?
objectives: Use binary storage units from bit to tebibyte (2.3.1)
Calculate image, sound and text file sizes
Calculate how many files fit in a given capacity
successCriteria: All: order the storage units and state the factor between them
Most: calculate an image or a sound file size in bytes and KiB
Some: calculate capacities and choose the right unit with correct conversion
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: powers, standard units and rates
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste (israf) of resources by storing only what is needed

keywords.def: 1024 bytes
1024 kibibytes
1024 mebibytes
1024 gibibytes
the amount of storage a file needs, measured in bits or bytes

starter: Bismillah. What is 2 to the power of 10?
How many bits are in 6 bytes?
Calculate 16 x 1024.

teach.heading: The units
bullets: Nibble: 4 bits. Byte: 8 bits
Each unit is 1024 times the one before
Bit, byte, KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB
teach.note: Say that 1024 is 2^10, so the binary units go up in powers of 2. Many devices and shops use kilobyte, megabyte and so on with factors of 1000, but this specification uses the binary names with factor 1024. Be ready for questions: always divide by 1024 when asked in KiB, MiB.

teach.heading: File size formulae
bullets: Image: width x height x colour depth (bits)
Sound: sample rate x bit depth x seconds (bits)
Divide bits by 8 for bytes; by 1024 for each larger unit
teach.note: Write the three-step routine on the board: calculate bits, convert to bytes, then to the unit asked for. State that for a mono recording we ignore channels unless the question says otherwise. Check units at the end.

code.text:
bits = 640 * 480 * 8
print(bits, "bits")
print(bits // 8, "bytes")
print(bits // 8 / 1024, "KiB")

teach.heading: Worked example: sound file
teach.note: Model the calculation using seconds and the formula. Notice how the numbers are chosen so that the answer works out exactly at 1000 KiB. Then ask pupils what would happen to the size if the bit depth were halved.

model.problem: A mono sound is recorded for 32 seconds at 16 000 Hz with a bit depth of 16. Calculate the file size in KiB.
model.answer: The file is 1000 KiB (a little under 1 MiB).

teach.heading: Capacity calculations
bullets: Capacity divided by file size gives the number of files
Convert both to the same unit first
Round down: you cannot store part of a file
teach.note: Work an example: how many 4 MiB photos fit in 16 GiB? Convert 16 GiB to MiB (16 x 1024 = 16 384) then divide by 4. Pupils often forget the conversion or round up.

code.text:
capacity_mib = 16 * 1024
photo_mib = 4
print(capacity_mib // photo_mib, "photos")
print(2048 / 1024, "MiB in 2048 KiB")

teach.heading: Check: units
teach.note: Answer D. 3 MiB = 3 x 1024 KiB = 3072 KiB. A uses 1000. B and C divide instead of multiplying: a larger unit is made of many of the smaller ones, so going to the smaller unit we multiply.

check.q: How many kibibytes are in 3 mebibytes?
check.why: 1 MiB = 1024 KiB, so 3 MiB = 3 x 1024 = 3072 KiB. 3000 uses a factor of 1000 (A); dividing instead of multiplying gives B or C.

practice: State how many bytes are in 5 KiB.
A 1-bit image is 100 x 80 pixels. Calculate its size in bytes.
How many 2 MiB songs fit on a 1 GiB memory card?
independent: Core: A photo is 1024 x 768 pixels with 24-bit colour. Calculate its size in bytes and in KiB.
Extend: A mono recording lasts 3 minutes at 8000 Hz with 8-bit samples. Calculate the size in KiB.
Stretch: A phone has 128 GiB of storage and 14 GiB is used by the system. How many 5 MiB photos fit in the rest? Show every conversion.
exit: Convert 4 GiB to MiB.
State the formula for the size of an uncompressed image.
lessons.homework: Find the file sizes of three files on a device and find how many of each would fit on a 32 GiB drive. Show conversions.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a conversion ladder diagram (multiply down, divide up by 1024). Stretch: ask for calculations with several unit changes. Note: y11 lesson 2 of the existing set uses 1000 for unit steps; this lesson follows the specification's binary units.

lessons.unit: Unit 2.3: Data: storage units and compression
lessons.title: Compression: lossless and lossy
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we make a file smaller without ruining it?
objectives: Explain why compression is needed (2.3.2)
Compare lossless and lossy methods
Apply run-length encoding as an example of lossless compression
successCriteria: All: state two reasons for compressing data
Most: compare lossless and lossy with an example of each
Some: encode data with RLE and justify which type to use for a given file
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: ratio, percentages and compression ratio
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair use of shared bandwidth and storage; being careful not to lose information others rely on

keywords.def: making a file smaller so it uses less storage or is quicker to send
compression where no data is lost and the original can be rebuilt exactly
compression that permanently removes some data to save more space
a lossless method that stores a repeated value once with a count

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the file size in bytes of a 100 x 100 image with an 8-bit colour depth.
Convert 5 MiB into KiB.
Name one file format you know that uses compression.

teach.heading: Why compress?
bullets: Less storage space used
Quicker to upload, download and stream
Less bandwidth, so lower cost
teach.note: Relate to everyday: a video call, a school email attachment, a streaming video. Pupils say 'it makes it better quality', which is wrong: compression makes files smaller. Note that compressed files must usually be decompressed before use.

left.title: Lossless
points: Smaller files, but not very small

teach.heading: Which to use?
bullets: Lossless: documents, program files, medical scans
Lossy: photos, music, video for viewing or listening
Lossy quality drops if compressed too much
teach.note: Ask: what happens if a spreadsheet is compressed with a lossy method? Numbers would change. Photos and music have detail that humans barely notice, so lossy methods remove that. Examples: ZIP and PNG are lossless; JPEG and MP3 are lossy. The exam asks for reasons, so link the method to the purpose.

head: File
Better choice
Reason
rows: Holiday photo for a web page
Small size, minor detail not noticed
A single changed bit can break it
Needs to fit within the bandwidth

teach.heading: Run-length encoding
bullets: Replace runs of the same value with count and value
Works best when there are long runs
Lossless: decode to get the original back
teach.note: Trace the code: WWWWBBBWWW becomes 4W3B3W, 10 characters reduced to 6. For AAAABBBCCD the result 4A3B2C1D saves only two characters, and ABCD becomes 1A1B1C1D, which is twice as long. Make the point that RLE can make data bigger if there are few repeats. Confirm against the spec whether RLE is the named example for your cohort.

teach.heading: Worked example: compression saving
teach.note: Model with a percentage saving. 6 MiB compressed to 1.5 MiB is a quarter of the size, so 4.5 MiB is saved, 75%. Remind pupils to say whether the method is lossy or lossless in the explanation, and give a reason for choosing it.

model.problem: A 6 MiB photo is saved as a 1.5 MiB JPEG. Calculate the percentage saved and state the type of compression, with a reason it is suitable.
steps: JPEG is lossy: some detail is permanently removed
Suitable because small loss of detail in a photo is hard to notice
model.answer: 75% saved; lossy compression, suitable for a photo for viewing.

teach.heading: Check: choosing the method
teach.note: Answer B. A medical scan must be recovered exactly, so lossless. A is wrong because lossy removes detail. C has the right idea but 'no compression at all' misses the point of the question. D mixes up the two terms.

check.q: A hospital stores X-ray images. Which type of compression is most suitable and why?
options: Lossy, because it gives the smallest files
Lossless, because no detail may be lost
None, because compression always loses detail
Lossy, because the images can be rebuilt exactly
check.why: A medical image must be reproduced exactly, so lossless is the right choice. Lossy removes data permanently (A, D); compression need not lose detail (C).

practice: Give two benefits of compressing a video before sending it.
Apply run-length encoding to AAAAABBBB and state the number of characters before and after.
Explain why a ZIP file of a document can be turned back into the exact document but a heavily compressed JPEG cannot be turned back into the original photo.
independent: Core: Compress a row of pixels BBBBBWWWWWWWWBB with RLE and decode 3R2G4R.
Extend: A 2.4 MiB MP3 was made from a 20 MiB recording. Calculate the percentage reduction and explain what has been lost.
Stretch: Describe a row of 12 pixels where RLE makes the data longer, and explain why this happens.
exit: Define lossless compression.
State one reason to use lossy compression for a streamed video.
lessons.homework: Look at the file sizes of a photo as a PNG and as a JPEG (or find the sizes online). Write 100 words on which you would use for a website and why.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a decoding worksheet with RLE pairs boxed. Stretch: ask for an evaluation of RLE on text with few repeated characters.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.1: Problem solving with programming: designing, reading and refining programs
lessons.title: From problem to program: decomposing, reading and converting designs
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you turn a written problem into a working Python program?
objectives: Use decomposition and abstraction to plan a program (6.1.1)
Read, analyse and refine a high-level program (6.1.2)
Convert pseudocode and flowcharts into Python (6.1.3)
successCriteria: All: identify the inputs, processes and outputs of a problem
Most: convert pseudocode or a flowchart into a working program
Some: refine a working program so that it is shorter, clearer or more general
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: formulae and problem solving
lessons.smsc: Moral: planning before acting (a habit of care) leads to better results

keywords.def: a structured, language-independent way of writing an algorithm
a diagram of an algorithm using standard symbols
improve a working program, for example to make it shorter, clearer or faster
a way of planning: what goes in, what is done, what comes out

starter: Bismillah. What are the three constructs used in every algorithm?
State a decomposition of the problem: a program that totals a shopping basket.
In a flowchart, what shape holds a decision?

teach.heading: Plan before you type
bullets: Decompose: what are the sub-tasks?
Abstract: which data do we need?
Write inputs, processes, outputs
teach.note: Paper 2 tasks are marked on whether the program works, so the plan is a short list: inputs, processes, outputs. Ask pupils what a till program for a canteen needs and what it can ignore. Link back to unit 1.1 for the vocabulary.

head: Part
Canteen till example
rows: Price of each item, number of items
Add prices, apply 10% staff discount if staff

teach.heading: Pseudocode to Python
bullets: SET becomes =
FOR ... FROM becomes for ... in range
SEND ... TO DISPLAY becomes print
teach.note: Show the pseudocode first, then the Python on the next slide. Exam papers define their own notation, so make sure pupils can read both. Common translation errors: forgetting that range stops before the end value, and forgetting the colon and indentation.

code.text:
SET total TO 0
FOR i FROM 1 TO 3
    SET price TO prices[i]
    SET total TO total + price
END FOR
SEND total TO DISPLAY

teach.heading: The Python version
bullets: Lists start at index 0
range(3) gives 0, 1, 2
Iterating over the list is simpler
teach.note: Trace the program. Highlight that the pseudocode counts from 1 but Python lists start from 0, so a direct translation needs care. The simplest refinement is to loop over the list itself. Ask pupils which version is easier to read.

code.text:
prices = [2.50, 1.20, 0.80]
total = 0
for price in prices:
    total = total + price
print(total)

teach.heading: Worked example: read, analyse, refine
teach.note: Model the three stages as separate steps: first trace to understand, then name the purpose, then refine. The refined version is shorter, easier to extend and uses a function; mention that refinement must not change the output. Point out that analysing code is a skill tested in Paper 2.

model.problem: Read: n = 4; a = n * 1; b = n * 2; c = n * 3; print(a + b + c). Describe what it does and refine it.
steps: Purpose: adds the first three multiples of n (n x 1, n x 2, n x 3)
Refine: use a loop, so that any number of multiples can be added
Code: total = 0; for k in range(1, 4): total = total + n * k
model.answer: Output 24 both ways. The refined loop is shorter and the 3 can be changed to any number.

teach.heading: Check: converting a loop
teach.note: Answer B. range(1, 6) gives 1 to 5, so the program prints 5 lines. A would be range(5) which gives 0 to 4. C forgets that the end is excluded; D is a common mistake of thinking range includes the last number.

check.q: Pseudocode: FOR i FROM 1 TO 5 SEND i TO DISPLAY. Which Python is the correct translation?
check.why: range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. range(5) starts at 0 and stops at 4 (A); range(1, 5) stops at 4 (C); range(6) includes 0 and stops at 5 (D).

practice: Write inputs, processes and outputs for a program that converts a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit.
Translate into Python: SET count TO 0, WHILE count < 3, SEND count TO DISPLAY, SET count TO count + 1.
Read: total = 0; for n in [3, 6, 9]: total = total + n; print(total / 3). State what it calculates and its output.
independent: Core: Write Python for: SET total TO 0; FOR each mark IN [55, 70, 85]; SET total TO total + mark; SEND total TO DISPLAY.
Extend: Convert a flowchart described as: Start, SET n TO 1, decision n > 5, No: print n x n and add 1 to n then loop back, Yes: End. Write the Python and its output.
Stretch: Refine this code so that it works for any length of list: a = marks[0]; b = marks[1]; c = marks[2]; print((a + b + c) / 3).
exit: State one thing a programmer plans before writing code.
Why does range(1, 4) not include 4?
lessons.homework: Choose a short problem (for example calculating the cost of a taxi ride). Write inputs, processes and outputs, then the Python program for it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a translation table (SET, FOR, WHILE, SEND) next to each statement in Python. Stretch: ask for a refined version with a function. This lesson focuses on Paper 2 programming; the flowchart and pseudocode basics are in the existing y10 lessons 2 and 3.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.1: Problem solving with programming: designing, reading and refining programs
lessons.title: Readable code, debugging and evaluating programs
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you make code that other people can read, test and trust?
objectives: Write readable code with layout, indentation, comments, meaningful names and whitespace (6.1.4)
Find and correct logic, syntax and runtime errors in Python (6.1.5)
Evaluate fitness for purpose and efficiency using test data (6.1.6)
successCriteria: All: add comments and good names to a short program
Most: debug a program using the error message and a trace
Some: write a test table and evaluate whether a program is fit for purpose
lessons.crossCurricular: English: clarity of writing for a reader
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah (trust) towards the next programmer and the user by writing honest, clear code

keywords.def: the name of a variable, constant or subprogram
a note in code, starting with #, ignored by the computer
spaces at the start of a line that show which block it belongs to
finding and fixing errors in a program
chosen inputs with expected results

starter: Bismillah. Name the three types of error.
What kind of error is caused by a missing colon after if?
Give an example of boundary test data for a number between 1 and 10.

teach.heading: Readable code
bullets: Meaningful names: mean_mark, not x
Comments explain why, not just what
Indentation shows structure; blank lines separate parts
teach.note: Compare the two versions of the same code. In Python, indentation is part of the syntax, but names, comments and spacing are about the human reader. Ask pupils which version they would rather mark. In an exam, comments help the examiner follow partial answers.

right.title: Easy to read
points: Purpose is clear at a glance

teach.heading: Same program, tidy
bullets: Same output as before
Comments say what and why
Names tell the reader the data
teach.note: Run it. The output is the same as the untidy version, 5.33, which shows that readability does not change behaviour. Point out the comment above each block. Note that too many comments for obvious lines are not helpful either.

code.text:
# mean of a list of marks
marks = [3, 9, 4]
total = 0

for mark in marks:
    total = total + mark

mean = total / len(marks)
print(round(mean, 2))

teach.heading: Debugging method
bullets: Read the error message and line number
Predict the output, then compare
Use print statements or a trace table
teach.note: Show the run: the error appears at the last line of the traceback and gives the type and a clue. Ask pupils how to fix it (change the index to 2, or loop through the list). The skill is reading the message, not guessing.

code.output:
9
4
IndexError: list index out of range

teach.heading: Worked example: test and evaluate
teach.note: Model creating a test table with expected results BEFORE running the program. Then evaluate against the requirements: fit for purpose means it does what it was asked, including for boundaries and invalid data. Efficiency: does it avoid needless repeated work?

model.problem: A program should accept an exam mark from 0 to 100 and output 'pass' for 50 or more. Design test data and judge whether if mark > 50 is fit for purpose.
steps: Running the code with 50: it prints fail, which does not match the expected pass
model.answer: Not fit for purpose: the boundary value 50 fails. Fix: use >= 50, and add validation for invalid marks.

teach.heading: Check: spotting the logic error
teach.note: Answer C. The loop never reaches the last item because range(len(marks) - 1) stops one short; the program runs without an error message, so it is a logic error. A syntax error (A) would stop the program starting and a runtime error (B) would crash it, but this program runs to the end.

check.q: for i in range(len(marks) - 1): total = total + marks[i]. The program is meant to total every mark but gives too low an answer. What is wrong?
options: A syntax error: the brackets are wrong
A runtime error: marks[i] does not exist
A logic error: the loop stops one item early
No error: the answer is correct
check.why: The loop misses the last item, so the answer is too small, but the program still runs: a logic error. It is not a syntax (A) or runtime error (B).

practice: Rewrite x=[4,5];y=0 with readable names, a comment and good layout.
Give two reasons why meaningful variable names matter.
A program that checks a password length of 8 to 12 characters uses len(pw) > 8 and len(pw) < 12. Give two test values that show the fault.
independent: Core: Rewrite this with good names, comments and spacing, and check the output is unchanged: a=[3,9,4];t=0;for x in a: t=t+x;print(round(t/len(a),2)) (set out as separate lines).
Extend: Debug this program and name each error type: marks = [3, 9, 4], then for i in range(1, 4) with no colon, then print(marks[i]) inside the loop. There are two errors.

Stretch: Write a test table with at least eight rows (normal, boundary, erroneous) for a program that accepts an age from 11 to 16. Include expected results, then evaluate a program whose condition is age > 11 and age < 16.
exit: Give two ways to make code more readable.
What is the purpose of test data with expected results?
lessons.homework: Write a short Python program that totals a list of numbers. Deliberately introduce one bug of each type in three copies and note how Python reports (or does not report) each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a debugging checklist (read message, find the line, predict, fix) and a word bank. Stretch: ask pupils to review a classmate's code for readability. Existing y10 lesson 7 introduced validation and testing; this lesson adds style, debugging and evaluation.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.2: Problem solving with programming: program structure and control
lessons.title: Program structure and control: sequence, selection, repetition and iteration
lessons.bigQuestion: How do the parts of a program fit together so it does what you intend?
objectives: Identify the structural components of a program (6.2.1)
Use sequence, selection, repetition and iteration in Python (6.2.2)
Explain the idea of a single entry and a single exit point
successCriteria: All: identify the main parts of a program
Most: write programs using if/elif/else, for and while
Some: nest structures correctly and justify the choice of loop
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: conditions and iterative procedures
lessons.smsc: Moral: discipline and order (nidham) in organising work

keywords.def: a loop that runs a set number of times, such as for
a loop that runs while a condition is true, such as while
one structure placed inside another
each block of code is entered at the top and left at the bottom

starter: Bismillah. What does the % operator do in Python?
Write an if statement that prints 'adult' when age is 18 or more.
What is the difference between for and while?

teach.heading: Parts of a program
bullets: Libraries imported at the top
Constants and global data
Subprogram definitions, then the main program
teach.note: Show the labelled program. A typical order: imports, constants, subprograms, main code. Comments label each part. The same structure scales from 10 lines to 10 000. Pupils often put definitions after the code that calls them, which fails in Python.

code.text:
import math                      # library

VAT = 0.2                        # constant

def gross(net):                  # subprogram
    return net * (1 + VAT)

def main():                      # main program
    prices = [10, 20, 35]
    for p in prices:
        print(p, math.ceil(gross(p)))

main()

teach.heading: Selection and repetition in Python
bullets: if / elif / else chooses one path
for repeats a known number of times
while repeats until a condition is false
teach.note: Trace the program: the first matching branch runs and the rest are skipped. Check that pupils see why 6 gives six and not even: the order of conditions matters. Ask what would happen if the % 2 test came first.

code.output:
1 odd
2 even
3 odd
4 even
5 odd
6 six

teach.heading: Single entry and exit
bullets: Every structure is entered at the top
And left at the bottom
Nested structures sit completely inside others
teach.note: Draw boxes around the loop and the if inside it to show nesting. Structured programs are easier to read, test and prove correct. Avoid jumping out of the middle with extra exits where a condition would do. The while loop below has one entry and one exit and the condition is the only way out.

code.text:
attempts = 0
correct = False
guesses = [4, 9, 7]
while not correct and attempts < len(guesses):
    if guesses[attempts] == 7:
        correct = True
    attempts = attempts + 1
print(correct, attempts)

teach.heading: Worked example: choose the right loop
teach.note: Model the decision: ask 'do we know how many times in advance?' If yes, for; if not, while. Link 'iteration over data' with for item in list. Keep the focus on the choice and the justification, because Paper 2 and Paper 1 both ask pupils to explain why a loop is suitable.

model.problem: Choose a loop for each task and justify: (a) print the 12 times table; (b) keep asking for a password until it is correct; (c) total the marks in a list.
steps: (a) 12 repeats is known: count-controlled, for i in range(1, 13)
(b) Number of attempts is unknown: condition-controlled, while not correct
(c) Visit every item: iteration over a data structure, for mark in marks
Check that each loop has one entry point and one exit point
model.answer: (a) for, (b) while, (c) for over the list.

teach.heading: Check: order of conditions
teach.note: Answer C. In an if/elif chain the first true branch is the only one that runs, so 6 gets 'six' because that test is first. If the % 2 test came first, 6 would be labelled 'even'.

check.q: In the program with n % 6 == 0 first, which label is printed for n = 6?
check.why: The first condition, n % 6 == 0, is true so 'six' is chosen and the elif branches are skipped. 'even' (A) would be printed only if the even test came first.

practice: List four structural parts of a program in the order they usually appear.
Write a for loop that prints the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
Write a while loop that doubles a variable starting at 1 until it is more than 100, then prints it.
independent: Core: Write a program that prints 'fizz' for each multiple of 3 from 1 to 15 and the number otherwise.
Extend: Write a program with a list of five marks and use iteration and selection to print the number of marks of 60 or more.
Stretch: Extend the guessing loop so that it also prints 'not found' if no guess was 7, still with one entry and one exit. Explain why a single exit makes the program easier to test.
exit: Which loop is used when you do not know how many times to repeat?
What is meant by nested selection inside a loop?
lessons.homework: Write a program with a library import, a constant, a function and a main loop, and label each structural part with a comment.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a program with sections cut apart to reorder and label. Stretch: ask for a nested loop program printing a multiplication grid.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.3: Problem solving with programming: data types, variables and strings
lessons.title: Data types, variables, constants and arrays in Python
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you choose the right container and type for each piece of data?
objectives: Use integer, real, Boolean and character types, and convert between them (6.3.1)
Use one- and two-dimensional structures in Python (6.3.1)
Use variables and constants appropriately (6.3.2)
successCriteria: All: name the data type of a value and use a variable
Most: choose a suitable type for given data and use casting
Some: process a 2D structure with nested loops and justify a choice of constant
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: integers, decimals and number types
lessons.smsc: Moral: accuracy with personal data (amanah): choosing the right type avoids errors in people's records

keywords.def: a whole number
a number with a decimal part
True or False
a single letter, digit or symbol (a string of length 1 in Python)
converting a value from one data type to another

starter: Bismillah. What is a constant?
Give the output of 17 // 5 and 17 % 5.
Give an example of a record with three fields.

teach.heading: Primitive types
bullets: Integer: 12. Real (float): 3.5
Boolean: True / False
Character / string: 'A', 'Salam'
teach.note: Run the code and read the type names. Python has no separate character type, so a character is a string of length 1; mention that exams may say 'character' where Python says str. A phone number must be a string: leading zeros would be lost as an integer and we never add phone numbers.

code.text:
count = 12
price = 3.5
is_open = True
initial = "A"
print(type(count), type(price))
print(type(is_open), type(initial))

teach.heading: Casting
bullets: int() removes the decimal part
float() makes a real; str() makes text
input() always gives a string
teach.note: Show that int(3.9) is 3, not 4: it truncates. A string of digits must be cast before arithmetic; '12' + 1 gives an error and '12' + '1' gives '121'. Link to input in the next lesson.

code.text:
print(int(3.9), int("12") + 1)
print("12" + "1")
print(float(7), str(7) + "!")
print(round(3.9))

teach.heading: Constants and one- and two-dimensional structures
bullets: Constants: names in capitals, never changed
1D list: one row. 2D list: rows of rows
Nested loops visit every cell
teach.note: Constants make the program easy to update: VAT_RATE appears once. Draw the 2D list as a grid and say 'row first'. Pupils often use one loop for a 2D list: show that for row in grid gives whole rows, so a second loop is needed to reach each value.

teach.heading: Worked example: choose the types
teach.note: Model by asking for each field: is it a number we calculate with? could it include a decimal? is it yes/no? Phone numbers and postcodes are strings. The grade is a character. Link the choices to what operations will be applied.

model.problem: A school record holds: name, age in years, fees owed in pounds and pence, whether the fees are paid, and a one-letter grade. Choose a data type for each and justify.
steps: Age in years: integer, a whole number
Fees: real (float), because pence are decimals
Paid: Boolean, since it is only yes or no
model.answer: string, integer, real, Boolean, character.

teach.heading: Check: data types
teach.note: Answer C. A phone number is never used in arithmetic and may start with 0, so a string. A would drop the leading 0. B is wrong because we do not add phone numbers. D is not suitable as there is no yes/no.

check.q: Which data type is most suitable for storing the telephone number 07712 345678?
check.why: A telephone number has a leading zero and spaces and we never calculate with it, so a string. An integer (A) would lose the leading zero; real (B) and Boolean (D) are unsuitable.

practice: State the data type of each: 'Hello', 25, 2.75, True.
Write a statement that stores 20% as a constant called DISCOUNT and another that uses it to reduce a price of 50.
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]. State grid[2][0] and the number of rows.
independent: Core: Write Python to store a pupil's name, age, height in metres and whether they are a prefect, using suitable types.
Extend: A 2D list stores three pupils' marks in four tests. Write nested loops to output each pupil's total.
Stretch: Explain what happens if you add the strings '15' and '5', and if you add the integer 15 and the string '5'. Write the code that makes the two numbers add correctly.
exit: State one difference between a variable and a constant.
Why is a phone number stored as a string?
lessons.homework: Write a short program with at least four variables of different types (including one constant) and print the type of each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a card sort of values and their type names. Stretch: ask for a 2D structure holding a timetable and a loop that prints each day's lessons.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.3: Problem solving with programming: data types, variables and strings
lessons.title: Manipulating strings
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a program search inside text and change it?
objectives: Find the length of a string and use positions (6.3.3)
Extract substrings with slicing
Change case and search for text
successCriteria: All: use len and position to read a character
Most: slice a string and convert case
Some: combine find and slicing to extract a part of a string
lessons.crossCurricular: English: spelling, word patterns and text analysis
lessons.smsc: Cultural: handling names respectfully, including capital letters and spelling, shows adab to the person

keywords.def: a sequence of characters
the number of characters in a string
position of a character, starting from 0
a part of a string
a way of taking a substring, such as word[0:3]

starter: Bismillah. What is the index of the first item of a list?
How do you make a for loop visit every item in a list?
State the type of 'A'.

teach.heading: Length and position
bullets: len(word) is the number of characters
word[0] is the first; word[-1] is the last
Indexes run from 0 to len - 1
teach.note: Write 'Bismillah' with an index above each letter so pupils can see it. The positions are the key idea: the last index is len - 1. Pupils get an 'index out of range' error by using len(word) as an index.

code.text:
word = "Bismillah"
print(len(word))
print(word[0], word[-1])
print(word[0:3])
print(word.upper(), word.lower())
print(word.find("mil"))

teach.heading: Slices, case and find
bullets: word[a:b] starts at a and stops before b
upper() and lower() convert case
find returns the position or -1
teach.note: In the run above, word[0:3] is 'Bis': positions 0, 1, 2. find gives the position where the substring starts, 3. If not found it returns -1: ask what that is useful for. Strings cannot be changed in place; we build new strings.

teach.heading: Looping over characters
bullets: for ch in text visits each character
Use in to test whether a letter is in a set
Convert to lower case before comparing
teach.note: Trace the vowel counter with 'Tarbiyyah': a, i, a is 3 vowels. Ask pupils why we lower-case first (so 'A' counts too). This pattern appears in Paper 2 tasks.

teach.heading: Worked example: extract the username
teach.note: Model by combining find and slicing. Ask where the at sign is (position 5 in 'amina@school.org'), so the username is the slice from 0 up to that position. Ask what the domain slice would be (from position 6).

model.problem: An email address is stored as email = 'amina@school.org'. Write code to output the part before the @ in capitals.
steps: Find the position of the @: at = email.find('@') gives 5
Slice from the start up to but not including position 5: email[0:at]
model.answer: The output is AMINA.

teach.heading: Check: slicing
teach.note: Answer B. keyboard has k0 e1 y2 b3 o4 a5 r6 d7, so [2:5] is positions 2, 3 and 4: 'ybo'. A is [1:4] and C is [2:6]; D is what you get by counting from 1.

check.q: word = 'keyboard'. What is word[2:5]?
check.why: Positions 2, 3 and 4 are y, b, o. The slice stops before position 5. 'eyb' starts at 1 (A); 'yboa' includes position 5 (C).

practice: For name = 'Zainab', state len(name), name[0] and name[1:4].
Write code to print a word in capitals and its length.
Write code that prints how many times the letter 'a' appears in 'Alhamdulillah'.
independent: Core: Write a program that prints the first and last letters of 'Madrasah' and its length.
Extend: Store 'Surname,Forename' as a string and use find and slicing to print Forename Surname.
Stretch: Write a program that checks whether a word is a palindrome (reads the same backwards), using slicing. Test with 'level' and 'salam'.
exit: What is the index of the last character of a 6-letter string?
State the difference between upper() and lower().
lessons.homework: Write a program that takes the sentence 'Learning is a path to Jannah' and prints the number of letters, the first word and the sentence in capitals.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give an indexed strip of letters for each example. Stretch: ask for a function that counts any given letter.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.4: Problem solving with programming: input, files, validation and authentication
lessons.title: Input and CSV files
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a program get data from a person, and keep it after it closes?
objectives: Accept and respond to user input (6.4.1)
Read from and write to CSV text files (6.4.2)
Process the lines of a file using split and casting
successCriteria: All: write a program that asks for input and responds
Most: write records to a CSV file and read them back
Some: process a CSV file to calculate a result such as a total or a highest value
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: data handling and tables
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah with other people's data: only keep what is needed and keep it safe

keywords.def: data entered into a program by the user
comma-separated values: a text file with fields separated by commas
data stored permanently on secondary storage
a string method that breaks a string into a list at a chosen character

starter: Bismillah. What data type does input() return?
Write a Python statement to convert the string '25' to an integer.
What is a record?

teach.heading: User input
bullets: input shows a prompt and returns a string
Cast the string to a number before arithmetic
Respond to what was entered
teach.note: Pupils type the line into Python; you may show the interaction on the table. The program cannot do arithmetic on a string, so int() is essential. Ask what happens if the user types 'abc' (a runtime error; validation comes in the next lesson).

teach.heading: Writing a CSV file
bullets: Open with 'w' to write (replaces the old file)
Each record is one line; fields are separated by commas
End each line with \n and close the file
teach.note: Show that a CSV file is just text. Mode 'a' adds to the end instead of replacing: ask what would happen if we used 'w' each time in a loop. Always close the file, or the data may not be saved. Note: the exam may supply its own file-handling pattern; check what the paper uses.

code.text:
file = open("scores.csv", "w")
file.write("Amina,72\n")
file.write("Bilal,58\n")
file.close()

file = open("scores.csv", "r")
for line in file:
    name, score = line.strip().split(",")
    print(name, int(score) + 5)
file.close()

teach.heading: Reading and splitting
bullets: strip removes the newline at the end
split(',') makes a list of fields
Fields are strings: cast the numbers
teach.note: Walk through the read half of the program. Pupils forget strip (the \n stays on the last field) and forget to cast. Ask what name and score hold on the first line: 'Amina' and '72'.

teach.heading: Worked example: highest score
teach.note: Model the loop with a running maximum. Emphasise casting the score to an integer: otherwise '9' > '58' compares as text and is True. Trace with the two records: Amina 72, then Bilal 58 is smaller.

model.problem: scores.csv has the lines Amina,72 and Bilal,58 and Sara,91. Describe the steps to output the name with the highest score.
steps: Set best_score to 0 and best_name to an empty string
For each line: strip, split on the comma, convert the score with int()
If the score is higher than best_score, update both variables
Close the file and print best_name
model.answer: The program outputs Sara, with 91.

teach.heading: Check: types after splitting
teach.note: Answer C. split always gives strings, even for digits. A and B would be correct only after int(). D is the whole line, which is before the split.

check.q: The line 'Sara,15,Y10' is read from a file and stored in line. After parts = line.split(','), what is parts[1]?
check.why: split gives a list of strings, so parts[1] is the string '15'. It becomes a number only after int(parts[1]). The whole line (D) is the value before splitting.

practice: Write two lines of Python that ask for a pupil's name and greet them.
Write the CSV line for a record: name Omar, age 14, form 9A.
Explain why the 'w' mode would delete earlier records if used each time you save one.
independent: Core: Write a program that asks for a name and a mark, then writes them to a CSV file on one line.
Extend: Write a program that reads scores.csv and outputs the total of all the scores.
Stretch: Write a program that reads a CSV file of name and score and writes a second file containing only the pupils with 60 or more.
exit: State what 'csv' stands for.
Why do we use strip() when reading lines?
lessons.homework: Create a small CSV (on paper) of five classmates' favourite numbers, then write the Python that reads it and prints the mean.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the file program with gaps to fill. Stretch: ask for error handling when the file is missing.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.4: Problem solving with programming: input, files, validation and authentication
lessons.title: Validation and authentication
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we stop bad data and bad users from getting into a program?
objectives: Apply validation: length, presence, range and pattern checks (6.4.3)
Apply authentication: ID and password, and lookup (6.4.4)
Explain the difference between validation and checking correctness
successCriteria: All: name the four validation checks
Most: write a function for each type of validation check
Some: write a login routine with a lookup and limited attempts
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: online safety and strong passwords
lessons.smsc: Moral: amanah and honesty: protect people's accounts and never store or share passwords carelessly

keywords.def: an automatic check that data is sensible and in the right form
tests that a value lies between a minimum and a maximum
tests the number of characters
tests that something was entered
proving who you are, for example with an ID and password

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between a syntax error and a logic error?
Write the condition: x is between 5 and 10 inclusive.
What does len('Salam') return?

teach.heading: Four validation checks
bullets: Presence: something was entered
Length: the right number of characters
Range: between a minimum and a maximum
teach.note: Pattern (format) check: the data follows a layout such as one letter then three digits. Validation tells us that data is reasonable, not that it is correct: a pupil aged 14 entered as 15 passes. Give pupils the table of checks and an example each.

teach.heading: Validation as functions
bullets: Each check returns True or False
Combine checks with and
Reuse them wherever data is entered
teach.note: Run the code and read the output in pairs. The pattern check uses string methods: isalpha and isdigit. Each function is short, testable and reusable (link to subprograms). Pupils often forget that the function returns a Boolean rather than printing.

code.output:
False True
False True
True False

teach.heading: Authentication by lookup
bullets: Look the user ID up in stored data
Compare the password for that ID
Limit the number of attempts
teach.note: Trace the program: the first attempt has the right ID and a wrong password, the second succeeds. Real systems never store plain passwords: they store a protected form (a hash). That is beyond this course, but the habit of never writing a password in plain text is a matter of amanah.

teach.heading: Worked example: validate and re-ask
teach.note: Model the loop pattern: ask, check, repeat while invalid. In an exam the structure matters more than the exact messages. Test with boundary data: 0 and 100 pass, -1 and 101 fail.

model.problem: Describe a program that asks for a mark from 0 to 100 and keeps asking until it is valid.
steps: Ask for the mark and convert it with int()
While the mark is below 0 or above 100: print an error message
Ask again inside the loop and convert again
After the loop ends, the mark is valid and can be used
model.answer: Code: mark = int(input('Mark: ')); while mark < 0 or mark > 100: print('Invalid'); mark = int(input('Mark: '))

teach.heading: Check: what validation can and cannot do
teach.note: Answer A. A range check can show the value is within limits but cannot know it is true. B would need the name to be a real person; C is verification; D is not a type of validation. Discuss why double entry (verification) is a separate idea.

check.q: A user enters their age as 51 instead of 15. The program has a range check from 11 to 16. What happens?
options: The program rejects it, because the value is outside the range
The program accepts it as correct
The program accepts it, but the data is wrong
The program rejects it, because it fails a pattern check
check.why: 51 is outside 11 to 16, so the range check rejects it. A range check would not catch 14 typed instead of 15, because validation tests that data is sensible, not that it is correct. A pattern check (D) tests layout, not size.

practice: Name the validation check that stops an empty username.
Write a Python function that returns True if a password is at least 8 characters.
Explain one reason why validated data may still be incorrect.
independent: Core: Write a validation routine for an age between 11 and 16 that keeps asking until valid.
Extend: Write a function valid_postcode that returns True if a string has length 6, begins with a letter and ends with a digit. Test it with three values.
Stretch: Write a login routine that allows three attempts, using a dictionary of users, and prints a message after a successful or failed login.
exit: List the four types of validation check.
State what authentication proves.
lessons.homework: Choose a form you use (a library card or school login). List every field and say which validation check you would use for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a matching task for check and example (and a function template). Stretch: ask for a function that combines several checks.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.5: Problem solving with programming: operators
lessons.title: Arithmetic, relational and logical operators in Python
lessons.bigQuestion: How do small operators like % and // solve big problems?
objectives: Use arithmetic operators including modulus, integer division and exponentiation (6.5.1)
Use relational operators (6.5.2)
Use logical operators AND, OR and NOT in conditions (6.5.3)
successCriteria: All: evaluate expressions using each operator
Most: use % and // to solve problems such as even/odd and time conversion
Some: combine operators with correct precedence in conditions
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: order of operations, remainders and indices
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the Arabic roots of the word algorithm (from al-Khwarizmi) and of algebra: a link between mathematics and computing

keywords.def: the remainder after division (% in Python)
division that discards the remainder (// in Python)
raising to a power (** in Python)
compares two values: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
the order in which operators are worked out

starter: Bismillah. Work out 3 + 4 x 2 and (3 + 4) x 2.
Complete the truth table row for True AND False.
What does == test in Python?

teach.heading: Arithmetic operators
bullets: + - * / as usual; / gives a real
// integer division, % remainder
** for powers, such as 2 ** 5
teach.note: Run the program. 17 // 5 is 3 (how many whole fives) and 17 % 5 is 2 (what is left over). Show 7 / 2 gives 3.5 but 7 // 2 gives 3. Brackets then ** then * / // % then + - is the order of precedence.

teach.heading: What % and // are used for
bullets: Even or odd: n % 2
Digits: n % 10 is the last digit
Time: // for whole units, % for the rest
teach.note: Model the time example below as a worked problem. Add: use % for 'every third' loops and for wrapping around (clock, days of week). Ask pupils to find the last digit of 4827 (7) and the number without it (482).

code.text:
seconds = 4000
hours = seconds // 3600
rest = seconds % 3600
minutes = rest // 60
secs = rest % 60
print(hours, minutes, secs)
print(4827 % 10, 4827 // 10)

teach.heading: Worked example: even and odd with %
teach.note: Model the idea: a remainder of 0 when dividing by 2 means even. The program is the heart of many Paper 2 tasks. Then add the relational and logical operators: and, or, not combine conditions. Note that and is worked out before or.

model.problem: Write a condition that is True when n is even and greater than 10, and trace it for n = 14 and n = 8.
steps: Combine with and: n % 2 == 0 and n > 10
n = 8: 8 % 2 = 0 (True) but 8 > 10 is False, so False
model.answer: The condition is n % 2 == 0 and n > 10. It is True for 14 and False for 8.

teach.heading: Misconception: and before or
bullets: and is worked out before or
True or False and False is True
Use brackets to show what you mean
teach.note: Run this in Python: print(True or False and False) gives True, because False and False is False and then True or False is True. With brackets (True or False) and False the answer is False. Brackets save marks.

misconception.wrong: True or False and False is False, because it is worked out left to right.
misconception.right: and is worked out first: False and False is False, then True or False is True. Brackets, (True or False) and False, would give False.

teach.heading: Check: evaluate
teach.note: Answer A. 3 ** 2 is 9, then 9 * 2 is 18, then plus 2 is 20. B ignores precedence (2 + 3) ** 2 * 2. C and D confuse ** with * or evaluate left to right.

check.q: What is the value of 2 + 3 ** 2 * 2 in Python?
check.why: ** is first: 3 ** 2 = 9, then 9 * 2 = 18, then 2 + 18 = 20. 50 comes from adding first, (2 + 3) ** 2 * 2 (B); 18 forgets to add the 2 (D).

practice: Write a condition that is True if a mark is between 40 and 60 inclusive.
Write Python code to convert 135 minutes into hours and minutes.
independent: Core: Write a program that loops from 1 to 20 and prints only the multiples of 4.
Extend: Write a program that takes a three-digit number such as 472 and prints its digits separately using // and %.
Stretch: A leap year is divisible by 4 but not by 100, unless divisible by 400. Write the condition with logical operators and test 1900, 2000 and 2024.
exit: What does 25 % 7 give?
State one use of integer division in a program.
lessons.homework: Write five different expressions that use %, // and ** and work out the results by hand. Check with Python.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give an operator card with symbol, name and example for each. Stretch: ask for the digit-sum of a four-digit number using a loop.

lessons.unit: Unit 6.6: Problem solving with programming: subprograms and scope
lessons.title: Subprograms: functions, procedures and scope
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you build a program from small, reusable pieces without them interfering?
objectives: Use built-in, library and user-defined subprograms (6.6.1)
Know that functions return values and procedures do not (6.6.2)
Use local and global variables appropriately (6.6.3)
successCriteria: All: name a built-in and a library subprogram and call a function
Most: write a function with parameters and a return value, and a procedure
Some: explain scope and predict the effect of local and global variables
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: functions with inputs and outputs
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility: each part of a program looks after its own job (amanah)

keywords.def: a subprogram that returns a value
a subprogram that does a job but does not return a value
a variable in the subprogram definition that receives a value
a variable that exists only inside the subprogram
a variable declared outside subprograms that can be seen everywhere

starter: Bismillah. State two benefits of subprograms.
What does len('Salam') return?
What does the keyword def do?

teach.heading: Three kinds of subprogram
bullets: Built-in: print, len, int, round
Library: import math, then math.sqrt(49)
User-defined: written by the programmer with def
teach.note: Show that the library must be imported before use. Libraries save writing code that experts have already tested; mention random (random numbers, not predictable, so no output here). The programmer decides when to write their own: when no existing one does the job.

code.text:
import math
print(len("Salam"), round(3.14159, 2))
print(math.sqrt(49), math.ceil(4.2))

teach.heading: Functions and procedures
bullets: Function: returns a value to the caller
Procedure: carries out a task, returns nothing
Parameters pass data in
teach.note: Run the program and discuss each line of output. The last line shows that a procedure has no useful return value (Python shows None). In the exam a function is called in an expression or assigned to a variable; a procedure is called on its own line.

code.text:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

def show(w, h):
    print("Area is", area(w, h))

result = area(3, 4)
print(result)
show(5, 2)
print(show(1, 1))

teach.heading: Local and global scope
bullets: Local: created inside, gone when it ends
Global: declared outside, visible everywhere
Prefer parameters and return to global variables
teach.note: Run the code: the error shows that bonus does not exist outside the function. Global variables can be changed from anywhere, which makes faults hard to find; passing values in through parameters is safer. Ask pupils why two subprograms can both have a local variable called i without clashing.

code.text:
total = 100

def add_bonus(points):
    bonus = 5
    return points + bonus

score = add_bonus(total)
print(score)
print(bonus)

teach.heading: Worked example: write a function
teach.note: Model naming, parameters, return and a call. Show that the function has no input or print inside: it does one job, and the caller decides what to do with the result. Test with the values given: 45 out of 60 is 75.0.

model.problem: Write a function percentage that takes a score and a total and returns the percentage rounded to one decimal place. Show a call for 45 out of 60.
steps: Return the rounded result: return round(result, 1)
model.answer: The call outputs 75.0.

teach.heading: Check: function or procedure?
teach.note: Answer D. The subprogram returns a value that is used in an expression, so it is a function. A and B describe a procedure. C is wrong: parameters do not decide the type.

check.q: def double(n): return n * 2. The statement y = double(8) is run. What is double?
options: A procedure, because it has a parameter
A procedure, because it is user-defined
